1:26

God said, "Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness, and let them rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and the livestock and all the earth and every crawling thing that crawls on the earth."

and-said God let-us-make human in-our-image like-our-likeness and-let-them-rule in-fish-of the-sea and-in-bird-of the-sky and-in-the-livestock and-in-all-of the-earth and-in-all-of the-crawler the-crawling on the-earth

Grammar
  • נַעֲשֶׂה is 1st person plural: Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take it as God speaking with the angels (Rashi: his court); the royal plural, which Ibn Ezra reports from the Gaon, he rejects. The English keeps 'us'.
  • אָדָם has no article, so 'a human' or 'humankind', not yet a name; the article comes in 1:27.
  • בְּצַלְמֵנוּ and כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ stand side by side with no ו: 'in our image, like our likeness'.
  • וְיִרְדּוּ is a plural jussive, so the one אָדָם is collective. The root רדה sounds like ירד, 'go down' (Rashi).
  • Five domains of rule are listed: fish, birds, livestock, all the earth, and crawling things.

The plural 'Let us make': Rashi takes it as God taking counsel with his heavenly court, to teach humility; Ibn Ezra rejects the Niphal reading and the Gaon's royal plural, and reads God speaking to the angels. The English keeps 'us'. 'Humankind' is used because אָדָם has no article and the following verb is plural; 1:27 then has הָאָדָם. 'All the earth' follows the Hebrew word for word; Radak reads it as the wild animals of the earth.

Commentary (27)
Rashinormativefollows נַֽעֲשֶׂ֥ה אָדָ֛ם
Rashi: we learn God's humility here. Since the human is in the likeness of the angels and they would be jealous, God consulted them; a king deciding a case consults his court, as in Micaiah's vision before Ahab. The English keeps 'us' as a true plural.

Ibn Ezranormativefollows נַֽעֲשֶׂ֥ה אָדָ֛ם
Ibn Ezra: some take נעשה as a Niphal participle (Neh 5:18) and 'in our image' as Moses' words; he calls this lacking sense. He reports the Gaon (image = rule; the plural is how kings speak, citing Gen 29:27, Dan 2:36, Num 22:6) and rejects those proof texts as 'false witnesses'. His own reading: God said to the angels, 'Let us make a human; we will busy ourselves with him, not the water and the earth'; the image is the human's upper soul, which does not die, and בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים means the image of an angel.

בַּעֲבוּר הֱיוֹתוֹ זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה אָמַר "וְיִרְדּוּ" בִּדְגַת הַיָּם לְשׁוֹן רַבִּים. וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (בראשית רבה ז':ה') אָמְרוּ, "תּוֹצֵא הָאָרֶץ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה לְמִינָהּ", אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר "נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה" זוֹ רוּחוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן. וְלֹא יִתָּכֵן שֶׁיֹּאמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר כִּי "תּוֹצֵא הָאָרֶץ" יִתְפָּרֵשׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן כְּלָל, אֶלָּא שֶׁיִּתְכַּוֵּן לְמָה שֶׁהִזְכַּרְתִּי, לוֹמַר כִּי יְצִירַת הָאָדָם בְּרוּחוֹ הוּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר בַּדָּם נַעֲשָׂה מִן הָאָרֶץ, כְּמַאֲמַר הַחַיָּה וְהַבְּהֵמָה, כִּי כָל נַפְשׁוֹת הַתְּנוּעָה נַעֲשׂוּ יַחַד, וְאַחַר כֵּן בָּרָא לָהֶם גּוּפוֹת. עָשָׂה תְּחִלָּה גּוּפֵי הַבְּהֵמָה וְהַחַיָּה וְאַחַר כָּךְ גּוּף הָאָדָם, וְנָתַן בּוֹ הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַזּוֹ וְאַחַר כֵּן נָפַח בּוֹ נְשָׁמָה עֶלְיוֹנִית, כִּי הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַנִּפְרֶדֶת אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ הִיא שֶׁנִּתְיַחֵד בָּהּ מַאֲמָר אַחֵר, אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר נְתָנָהּ, כְּדִכְתִיב (בראשית ב':ז') "וַיִּפַּח בְּאַפָּיו נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים". וְדֶרֶךְ הָאֱמֶת בַּפָּסוּק הַזֶּה יִוָּדַע לַמַּשְׂכִּיל בַּפָּסוּק הַשֵּׁנִי, וְאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁנִּתְכַּוֵּן לוֹ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר וְדָרַשׁ בְּ"תוֹצֵא הָאָרֶץ" אֶרֶץ הַחַיִּים, שֶׁתּוֹצֵא נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה לְמִינָהּ לְעוֹלָם עוֹמֶדֶת. וְכֵן מָה שֶׁאָמַר "זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם" (להלן א כז, להלן ה ב), כִּי הָיְתָה הַבְּרִיאָה מִתְּחִלָּה מִזָּכָר וּנְקֵבָה, וְנִשְׁמָתוֹ כְּלוּלָה בָּהֶם, אֲבָל הַיְּצִירָה הָיְתָה יְצִירָה לָאָדָם וּבִנְיַן צֵלָע לָאִשָּׁה, כַּאֲשֶׁר יְסַפֵּר בַּסּוֹף. וְלָכֵן הִזְכִּיר כָּאן "בְּרִיאָה" וּבַפָּרָשָׁה שֶׁל מַטָּה הִזְכִּיר "יְצִירָה", וְהַמַּשְׂכִּיל יָבִין. וְטַעַם "וְיִרְדּוּ", שֶׁיִּמְשְׁלוּ בְּחָזְקָה בַּדָּגִים וּבָעוֹף וּבַבְּהֵמָה וּבְכָל הָרֶמֶשׂ, וְהַ"בְּהֵמָה" תִּכְלֹל הַחַיָּה. וְאָמַר "וּבְכָל הָאָרֶץ", שֶׁיִּמְשְׁלוּ בָּאָרֶץ עַצְמָהּ, לַעֲקֹר וְלִנְתֹּץ וְלַחְפֹּר וְלַחְצֹב נְחֹשֶׁת וּבַרְזֶל. וּלְשׁוֹן "רְדִיָּה", מֶמְשֶׁלֶת הָאָדוֹן בְּעַבְדּוֹ:

בִּשְׁאָרֵי בְּרוּאֵי מַטָּה אָמַר ״תַּדְשֵׁא הָאָרֶץ״, ״יִשְׁרְצוּ הַמַּיִם״, ״תּוֹצֵא הָאָרֶץ״, וּכְשֶׁבָּא לִבְרֹא אֶת הָאָדָם שֶׁהוּא הַמֻּרְכָּב בָּאֲחֵרוֹת אָמַר ״נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם״, וּלְמַעֲלַת הָאָדָם וְלִכְבוֹדוֹ בְּרָאוֹ בָּאַחֲרוֹנָה לְהוֹדִיעַ שֶׁכָּל נִבְרְאֵי מַטָּה נִבְרְאוּ בַּעֲבוּרוֹ, וְשָׂמוּהוּ אָדוֹן עַל כֻּלָּם; וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר

בִּלְשׁוֹן רַבִּים פֵּרְשׁוּ אֲדֹנִי אָבִי זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה, כִּי כְּנֶגֶד הַיְסוֹדוֹת אָמַר שֶׁמִּכֹּחָם יָצְאוּ הַנִּבְרָאִים וּבִרְצוֹן הָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״תַּדְשֵׁא״, ״יִשְׁרְצוּ״, ״תּוֹצֵא״, וּכְאִלּוּ אָמַר לַיְסוֹדוֹת, נַעֲשֶׂה אֲנִי וְאַתֶּם בְּשִׁתּוּף, כִּי הַגּוּף יִהְיֶה מִן הַיְסוֹדוֹת וּבְרוּחוֹ יִהְיֶה עֶלְיוֹנִי כְּמוֹ הַמַּלְאָכִים; וְכֵן מָצָאנוּ בְּדִבְרֵי חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בראשית רבה פ״ח) בִּמְלֶאכֶת שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ נִמְלַךְ; וְיֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים כִּי כְּנֶגֶד הַמַּלְאָכִים אָמַר שֶׁהֵם שְׂכָלִים נִפְרָדִים אָמַר נַעֲשֶׂה בָּאָרֶץ נוֹצָר אֶחָד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ חֵלֶק עֶלְיוֹנִי מִמֶּנּוּ, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ שֵׂכֶל נִפְרָדִי, וְכֵן מָצָאנוּ בְּדִבְרֵי חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בראשית רבה פ״ח) בְּמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת נִמְלַךְ, וְאָמְרוּ ״לִמְּדָה תּוֹרָה דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גָּדוֹל נִמְלָךְ בְּקָטָן מִמֶּנּוּ״ וְעוֹד אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָן בְּשֵׁם רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהָיָה מֹשֶׁה כּוֹתֵב אֶת הַתּוֹרָה הָיָה כּוֹתֵב מַעֲשֵׂה כָּל יוֹם וָיוֹם כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְפָסוּק זֶה נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם אָמַר לְפָנָיו רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם מָה אַתָּה נוֹתֵן פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה לַמִּינִים? אָמַר לוֹ כְּתֹב וְהָרוֹצֶה לִטְעוֹת יִטְעֶה. וְקָרָא אוֹתוֹ אָדָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם״ וְאָמַר (בראשית ה:א) ״וַיִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמָם אָדָם״, וְאָדָם הוּא לָקוּחַ מֵהָאֲדָמָה, וְאִם כֵּן לָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ אָדָם כִּי גַּם הַחַיִּים הָאֲחֵרִים הֵם מֵאֲדָמָה? אֶלָּא רָצָה לְהַבְדִּילוֹ בִּשְׁמוֹ מִשְּׁאָר בַּעֲלֵי הַחַיִּים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁהוּא מֻבְדָּל מֵהֶם בָּרוּחַ וּבַגּוּף, כִּי הַחַיִּים הָאֲחֵרִים יְדוּעִים כִּי הֵם מֵאֲדָמָה רוּחָם וְגוּפָם וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לְיַחֲסָם לָאֲדָמָה אֲבָל אָדָם שֶׁרוּחוֹ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם קָרָא אוֹתוֹ אָדָם לְהַבְדִּילוֹ מֵחַיִּים הָעֶלְיוֹנִים שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק כְּלָל מֵאֲדָמָה, וְאֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר אוֹתָם שֶׁאֵינָם גּוּפוֹת שֶׁהֵם כֻּלָּם רוּחָנִיִּים, אֶלָּא אֲפִלּוּ אוֹתָם שֶׁהֵם בַּעֲלֵי גוּף, אֵין גּוּפָם מֵאֲדָמָה כְּלָל, וְאֵין יְסוֹדָם מֵאַרְבַּע יְסוֹדוֹת שֶׁהֵם אַדְמִיִּים כִּי הֵם יְסוֹד חֲמִישִׁי כְּמוֹ שֶׁחָקְרוּ בַּעֲלֵי הַמֶּחְקָר, וּכְשֶׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶת הָאָדָם מֵהָעֶלְיוֹנִים וְהַתַּחְתּוֹנִים קְרָאוֹ אָדָם, כְּלוֹמַר אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁרוּחוֹ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם אָדָם הוּא כִּי גוּפוֹ נוֹצַר מִן הָאֲדָמָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר עָפָר מִן הָאֲדָמָה, וּמוֹשָׁבוֹ בָּאֲדָמָה וְשָׁם חַיּוּתוֹ וְתַרְבּוּתוֹ, וְלֹא יִטֶּה לְצַד עֶלְיוֹן אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ אֶלָּא אֶחָד מִנִּי אֶלֶף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר שְׁלֹמֹה (קהלת ז:כח) ״אָדָם אֶחָד מֵאֶלֶף מָצָאתִי״.

. וְאִם נְפָרֵשׁ

כְּנֶגֶד הַמַּלְאָכִים יִהְיֶה הַפֵּירוּשׁ צֶלֶם וּדְמוּת רוּחָנִי, כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁנָּשִׂים בּוֹ חֵלֶק מִצַּלְמוּתֵינוּ וּמִדְּמוּתֵינוּ שֶׁהוּא צֶלֶם וּדְמוּת רוּחָנִי, כִּי צֶלֶם וּדְמוּת שֵׁמוֹת מְשֻׁתָּפִים, וְאָמַר צֶלֶם בְּדָבָר גַּשְׁמִי כְּמוֹ (שמואל א ו:ה) ״צַלְמֵי טְחֹרֵיכֶם״, ״צַלְמֵי מַסֵּכוֹתָם״ (במדבר לג:נב), וְהַדּוֹמִים לָהֶם, וְיֵאָמֵר גַּם כֵּן בְּדָבָר רוּחָנִי, כְּמוֹ ״בְּצַלְמֵנוּ״, ״בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים״, וְכֵן דְּמוּת יֵאָמֵר לְדָבָר גַּשְׁמִי, כְּמוֹ (שיר השירים ז:ח) ״קוֹמָתֵךְ דָּמְתָה לְתָמָר״, וְהַדּוֹמִים לוֹ, וּלְדָבָר רוּחָנִי ״וּדְמוּת הַחַיּוֹת״, כְּמוֹ (יחזקאל לב:ב) ״כְּפִיר גּוֹיִם נִדְמֵיתָ״. ״דָּמִיתִי לְקָאַת מִדְבָּר״ (תהלים קב:ז) בְּעִנְיָן לֹא בְּגוּף, וְכֵן הַדּוֹמִים לָהֶם, וְעִנְיַן נַעֲשֶׂה לְפִי שֶׁהֵם בָּאֶמְצָעִיִּים, וּבֵי״ת בְּצַלְמֵנוּ יִהְיֶה בֵּית הָעֵזֶר, כְּלוֹמַר עִם צַלְמֵנוּ, שֶׁהוּא הַשֵּׂכֶל, נַעֲשֶׂה וּנְתַקֵּן אוֹתוֹ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא מִן הָאֲדָמָה, אוֹ תִּהְיֶה הַבֵּי״ת בֵּית כְּלִי כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּעִנְיַן נַעֲשֶׂה בְּשֵׂכֶל, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אֶחָד מֵחֶלְקֵי הַשֵּׂכֶל.

כְּלוֹמַר לָמָּה נַעֲשֶׂה בְּצַלְמֵנוּ, כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דּוֹמֶה לָנוּ שֶׁיִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּשִׂכְלִיּוֹת, וְתִהְיֶה כַּ״ף כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ כַּ״ף הַדִּמְיוֹן שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל לִהְיוֹת דְּמוּתֵנוּ מַמָּשׁ, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דּוֹמֶה לָנוּ בְּכָל חֲלָקָיו מִפְּנֵי חֵלֶק הֶעָפָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ, אֶלָּא יִהְיֶה דּוֹמֶה לִדְמוּתֵנוּ שֶׁיִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּשִׂכְלִיּוֹת, לְפִי הַכֹּחַ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לוֹ בְּעוֹדֶנּוּ גּוּף וְהוּא בָּאֲדָמָה, כִּי אִם יִרְצֶה יוּכַל לְהִדָּמוֹת קְצָת אֵלֵינוּ כִּי בְּיָדוֹ תִּהְיֶה הַבְּחִירָה, וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר שְׁלֹמֹה (קהלת ז:כט) ״אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה אֱלֹהִים אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר״ רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר יָשָׁר, שָׁוֶה וְיָשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲדִיף חֵלֶק אֶחָד עַל חֲבֵרוֹ כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּנַח כָּל אֶחָד מֵהֶם, כִּי זֶה עִנְיַן יָשָׁר, וְהָאֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אוֹתוֹ שִׂכְלִי וְעַפְרִי כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּכָל אֶחָד כְּפִי הָרָאוּי לוֹ, יִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּשֵׂכֶל כְּדֵי חַיּוּתוֹ וּבְעָפָר כְּדֵי חַיּוּתוֹ, בְּעָפָר כְּדֵי חַיּוּתוֹ לְבַד לֹא לְמוֹתָרוֹת וּלְהַשְׁאִיר מִינוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּבְשֵׂכֶל כְּדֵי חַיּוּתוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא; וְאָמַר (שם) ״וְהֵמָּה בִקְשׁוּ חִשְׁבֹּנוֹת רַבִּים״ כְּלוֹמַר, בִּקְשׁוּ אוֹתָם שֶׁהֵם חֶשְׁבֹּנוֹת רַבִּים, וְהֵם הַתַּאֲווֹת הֶעַפְרִיּוֹת, וְעָשׂוּ הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן שֶׁהוּא אֶחָד, וְהוּא הַשֵּׂכֶל, רַבִּים, וְהִנֵּה אֵינֶנּוּ יָשָׁר כִּי כֹּחַ הֶעָפָר מַכְרַעַת וְנִשְׁאַר הַמִּסְכֵּן וְחָכְמָתוֹ בְּזוּיָה, וְאָדָם לֹא זָכַר אֶת הָאִישׁ הַמִּסְכֵּן הַהוּא.

Apparatus
  • Plural 'us': Rashi (God and his court) and Ibn Ezra (God and the angels) agree; the royal plural of the Gaon, reported and rejected by Ibn Ezra, is not adopted.
  • Radak reads 'all the earth' as 'the wild animals of the earth'; this is not adopted in the English.
1:27

God created the human in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.

and-created God [object-mark] the-human in-his-image in-image-of God created him male and-female created them

Grammar
  • The verse has three lines: God created the human in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
  • הָאָדָם now has the article: it points back to the indefinite אָדָם of 1:26. It is not yet a proper name.
  • The object suffix changes from singular (אֹתוֹ) to plural (אֹתָם): one human, then male and female.
  • The first בָּרָא is a wayyiqtol; the next two are qatal and restate the act.
  • בְּצַלְמוֹ and בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים use the same noun: 'his image' and 'the image of God'.

The suffix of 'in his image' could refer to God or to the human; Rashi takes the image as a mold made for the human, and says that mold is the likeness of his maker. The English keeps 'his', as the Hebrew does. 'Male and female' is read as the plain sense that both were created on the sixth day.

Commentary (10)
Rashinormativefollows וַיִּבְרָ֨א אֱלֹהִ֤ים אֶת הָֽאָדָם֙ בְּצַלְמ֔וֹ
Rashi: 'in a mold made for him'; everything was created by word, but the human by hands (Ps 139:5); he was made with a seal, like a coin struck with a die. The English keeps 'in his image'; the mold sense goes in the notes.

Apparatus
  • The suffix of בְּצַלְמוֹ ('in his image') is not fixed by the Hebrew: God or the human. The next clause names God.
1:28

God blessed them, and God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and every living thing that crawls on the earth."

and-blessed [object-mark]-them God and-said to-them God be-fruitful and-multiply and-fill [object-mark] the-earth and-subdue-it and-rule in-fish-of the-sea and-in-bird-of the-sky and-in-all-of living the-crawling on the-earth

Grammar
  • The blessing is stated first (וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם), then the speech (וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם); the zinor and segol close the blessing sentence.
  • The imperatives are all plural: פְּרוּ, רְבוּ, מִלְאוּ, כִבְשֻׁהָ, רְדוּ.
  • וְכִבְשֻׁהָ is written without the second ו of the verb form; Rashi draws a lesson from the spelling.
  • After the etnaḥta on וְכִבְשֻׁהָ, the second half opens with וּרְדוּ: rule over three domains, fish, birds and every living thing that crawls, where 1:26 listed five.
  • חַיָּה הָרֹמֶשֶׂת has a feminine participle, where 1:26 had masculine הָרֹמֵשׂ.

The pack parses פְּרוּ as Qal, while its BDB extract lists only Hiphil senses, so no sense is given; the translation is 'be fruitful' either way. Rashi's reading of the defective וְכִבְשֻׁהָ is a homily on the spelling.

Commentary (13)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וְכִבְשֻׁ֑הָ
Rashi: וכבשה lacks a ו to teach that the male subdues the female so that she will not be a gadabout, and that the man, who is used to subduing, is commanded to be fruitful and multiply, not the woman. This is drawn from the spelling and does not change the English 'subdue it'.

Hebrew

1:29

God said, "See, I have given you every plant bearing seed that is on the surface of the whole earth, and every tree that has in it fruit of a tree bearing seed. It shall be yours for food."

and-said God see I-have-given to-you [object-mark] all-of herb sowing seed which on face-of all-of the-earth and-[object-mark] all-of the-tree which-in-it fruit-of tree sowing seed to-you it-shall-be for-food

Grammar
  • הִנֵּה with the qatal נָתַתִּי presents a gift already made: 'See, I have given'. Radak: as if 'I hereby give', or 'when I created them, I gave them to you'.
  • עֵשֶׂב זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע and פְּרִי־עֵץ זֹרֵעַ זָרַע are parallel, each a participle with its cognate noun: 'seed-sowing seed'.
  • The zaqef qaton on הָאָרֶץ divides the plants from the trees; the revia on זֶרַע sets off the relative clause אֲשֶׁר עַל־פְּנֵי כָל־הָאָרֶץ; the etnaḥta on זָרַע ends the gift.
  • יִהְיֶה is singular: 'it shall be', with the whole gift as one subject, not each plant.
  • לְאָכְלָה is 'for food'; the commentators note that this verse does not yet allow meat.

The verb זֹרֵעַ is 'sowing' and the English 'bears seed' renders the sense; the cognate noun is in English 'seed'. The commentators agree that the gift is plants only; the English says nothing about meat, which is not in the Hebrew.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativefollows לָכֶ֥ם יִֽהְיֶ֖ה לְאׇכְלָֽה׃
Rashi: he put cattle and wild animals on a par with them in food, and did not allow the human and his wife to kill a creature and eat flesh; all of them together were to eat only green herbs. When the sons of Noah came, he permitted flesh to them (Gen 9:3). The English 'for food', with plants alone, follows this.
Hebrew
הִשְׁוָה לָהֶם בְּהֵמוֹת וְחַיּוֹת לְמַאֲכָל, וְלֹא הִרְשָׁה לְאָדָם וּלְאִשְׁתּוֹ לְהָמִית בְּרִיָּה וְלֶאֱכֹל בָּשָׂר, אַךְ כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב יֹאכְלוּ יַחַד כֻּלָם, וּכְשֶׁבָּאוּ בְנֵי נֹחַ הִתִּיר לָהֶם בָּשָׂר, שֶׁנֶאֱמַר כָּל רֶמֶשׂ אֲשֶׁר הוּא חַי וְגוֹ' כְּיֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב שֶׁהִתַּרְתִּי לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן נָתַתִּי לָכֶם אֶת כֹּל:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֗ים הִנֵּה֩ נָתַ֨תִּי לָכֶ֜ם
Ibn Ezra: he permitted people, and everything with a living soul, to eat every herb; every tree fruit is permitted to people; the green herb is for the animals and for everything that crawls; meat was not permitted until after the flood. The English follows: the human has the plants and the fruit.

(רש"י על בראשית א':כ"ט) וְכֵן פֵּרֵשׁ הָרַב בְּמַסֶּכֶת סַנְהֶדְרִין (נט ד"ה לא הותר), "וּלְכָל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ", לָכֶם וְלַחַיּוֹת נָתַתִּי הָעֲשָׂבִים וְאֶת הָאִילָנוֹת וְ"אֶת כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב לְאָכְלָה". וְאִם כָּךְ יִהְיֶה פֵּרוּשׁ "אֶת כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב לְאָכְלָה" "וְאֶת כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב". וְאֵינוֹ כֵן, אֲבָל נָתַן לְאָדָם וּלְאִשְׁתּוֹ "כָּל עֵשֶׂב זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע" וְכָל פְּרִי עֵץ, וּלְחַיַּת הָאָרֶץ וּלְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם נָתַן "כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב", לֹא פְּרִי הָעֵץ וְלֹא הַזְּרָעִים, וְאֵין מַאֲכָלָם יַחַד כֻּלָּם בְּשָׁוֶה, אַךְ הַבָּשָׂר לֹא הֻרְשׁוּ בּוֹ עַד בְּנֵי נֹחַ כְּדַעַת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ, וְהוּא פְּשׁוּטוֹ שֶׁל מִקְרָא. וְהָיָה זֶה מִפְּנֵי שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי נֶפֶשׁ הַתְּנוּעָה יֵשׁ לָהֶם קְצָת מַעֲלָה בְּנַפְשָׁם, נִדְמוּ בָּהּ לְבַעֲלֵי הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַמַּשְׂכֶּלֶת, וְיֵשׁ לָהֶם בְּחִירָה בְּטוֹבָתָם וּמְזוֹנֵיהֶם וְיִבְרְחוּ מִן הַצַּעַר וְהַמִּיתָה, וְהַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר "מִי יוֹדֵעַ רוּחַ בְּנֵי הָאָדָם הָעֹלָה הִיא לְמָעְלָה וְרוּחַ הַבְּהֵמָה הַיֹּרֶדֶת הִיא לְמַטָּה לָאָרֶץ" (קהלת ג כא). וְכַאֲשֶׁר חָטְאוּ וְהִשְׁחִית כָּל בָּשָׂר אֶת דַּרְכּוֹ עַל הָאָרֶץ, וְנִגְזַר שֶׁיָּמוּתוּ בַּמַּבּוּל וּבַעֲבוּר נֹחַ הִצִּיל מֵהֶם לְקִיּוּם הַמִּין נָתַן לָהֶם רְשׁוּת לִשְׁחֹט וְלֶאֱכֹל כִּי קִיּוּמָם בַּעֲבוּרוֹ. וְעִם כָּל זֶה לֹא נָתַן לָהֶם הָרְשׁוּת בַּנֶּפֶשׁ וְאָסַר לָהֶם אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי. וְהוֹסִיף לָנוּ בַּמִּצְוֹת לֶאֱסֹר כָּל דָּם מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהוּא מַעֲמָד לַנֶּפֶשׁ, כְּדִכְתִיב (ויקרא יז יד) "כִּי נֶפֶשׁ כָּל בָּשָׂר דָּמוֹ בְנַפְשׁוֹ הוּא, וָאֹמַר לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל: דַּם כָּל בָּשָׂר לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ כִּי נֶפֶשׁ כָּל בָּשָׂר דָּמוֹ הִוא", כִּי הִתִּיר הַגּוּף בְּחַי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְדַבֵּר אַחַר הַמִּיתָה, לֹא הַנֶּפֶשׁ עַצְמָהּ. וְזֶה טַעַם הַשְּׁחִיטָה, וּמָה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (ב"מ לב) "צַעַר בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים דְּאוֹרָיְתָא", וְזוֹ בִּרְכָתֵנוּ שֶׁמְּבָרֵךְ "אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל הַשְּׁחִיטָה". וְעוֹד אֲדַבֵּר בְּעִנְיַן הַמִּצְוָה בַּדָּם בְּהַגִּיעִי שָׁם (ויקרא יז יא-יד) אִם גּוֹמֵר הַשֵּׁם עָלַי. וְטַעַם "אֶת כָּל עֵשֶׂב זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע וְאֶת כָּל הָעֵץ אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ פְרִי עֵץ זֹרֵעַ זָרַע לָכֶם יִהְיֶה לְאָכְלָה", שֶׁיֹּאכְלוּ זֵרוּעֵי הָעֵשֶׂב, כְּגַרְגְּרֵי הַחִטָּה וְהַשְּׂעוֹרָה וְהַקִּטְנִיּוֹת וְזוּלָתָם, וְיֹאכְלוּ כָּל פְּרִי הָעֵץ, אֲבָל הָעֵץ עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ לָהֶם לְאָכְלָה, וְגַם לֹא הָעֵשֶׂב, עַד שֶׁנִּתְקַלֵּל אָדָם וְנֶאֱמַר לוֹ: "וְאָכַלְתָּ אֶת עֵשֶׂב הַשָּׂדֶה" (בראשית ג':י"ח).

1:30

And to every wild animal of the earth and to every bird of the sky and to everything that crawls on the earth, in which there is a living soul, I have given every green plant for food. And so it was.

and-to-all-of animal-of the-earth and-to-all-of bird-of the-sky and-to-all-of crawling on the-earth which-in-it soul living [object-mark] all-of green herb to-food and-was so

Grammar
  • The verse has no verb of giving; it takes נָתַתִּי from 1:29 and אֶת marks its object.
  • The three groups are the same as in 1:26 and 1:28: wild animals, birds, crawling things; here without fish.
  • אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, 'in which is a living soul', describes the animals as having the breath of life, which the plants they eat do not have (Radak).
  • The telisha gedola on הָאָרֶץ is a rare doubled accent mark.
  • The English adds 'I have given' where the Hebrew has an object marker and no verb.

The Hebrew leaves out the verb 'I have given', so the English supplies it from 1:29 in the phrase that holds the object marker. The relative clause 'in which there is a living soul' stands after 'everything that crawls on the earth' and the English keeps it there; it can be read of all three groups.

Apparatus
  • The relative clause 'in which is a living soul' could limit only the crawling things or the three groups together; the English keeps the Hebrew order.
1:31 · פ

God saw everything that he had made, and indeed it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.

and-saw God [object-mark] all-of which he-made and-behold-good very and-was evening and-was morning day-of the-sixth

Grammar
  • The refrain of the days is 'and there was evening and there was morning', here with 'the sixth day', which is the only day in this chapter with the article.
  • וְהִנֵּה־טוֹב מְאֹד adds 'very' and וְהִנֵּה to the refrain 'and God saw that it was good' of the earlier days.
  • The qatal עָשָׂה ('he had made') looks back over the whole of the six days.
  • In יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי the ordinal has the article and יוֹם does not. The pack parses יוֹם as construct; Ibn Ezra reads 'the day that is sixth', a noun followed by an articled adjective, as in אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי (Lev 24:10).
  • The paragraph mark פ closes the account of the sixth day.

The article on 'the sixth' day is the Hebrew's, and the English follows it with 'the sixth day'. Rashi's homily on the added ה (the sixth day of Sivan, the giving of the Torah) does not bear on the plain sense.

Commentary (17)
Rashinormativenot-applicable י֥וֹם הַשִּׁשִּֽׁי׃
Rashi: the added ה on יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי means God made a condition with creation that Israel would accept the five books of the Torah; or: everything hangs until the sixth of Sivan. This is homily and does not bear on the English.

הוֹסִיף ה' בַּשִּׁשִּׁי בִגְמַר מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית, לוֹמַר שֶׁהִתְנָה עִמָּהֶם, עַל מְנָת שֶׁיְּקַבְּלוּ עֲלֵיהֶם יִשְׂרָאֵל חֲמִשָּׁה חֻמְּשֵׁי תוֹרָה. דָּבָר אַחֵר יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי, כֻּלָּם תְּלוּיִם וְעוֹמְדִים עַד יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי, הוּא ו' בְּסִיוָן הַמּוּכָן לְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַיַּ֤רְא
Ibn Ezra: some say יוֹם in יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי is in the construct state (סמוך) and the sense is 'the day of the sixth sphere'; this is not true. It means the day that is sixth from the first day, so also יוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי: a noun followed by an adjective with the article, as אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי (Lev 24:10), and רְקִיעַ הַשָּׁמַיִם (1:20), 'the firmament that is heaven'. The English 'the sixth day' follows this.

Apparatus
  • The paragraph mark פ follows this verse.
2:1

So the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their host.

and-were-completed the-heavens and-the-earth and-all-of host-their

Grammar
  • וַיְכֻלּוּ is Pual (passive): the heavens and earth 'were completed', with no agent named.
  • The wayyiqtol וַ + יְכֻלּוּ continues the narrative of chapter 1 and closes it.
  • The tevir on וַיְכֻלּוּ and the tipḥa on וְהָאָרֶץ divide the verse; the silluq ends it.
  • צְבָאָם ('their host') is normally an army or the stars; here it covers everything that fills heaven and earth.

'So' renders the narrative waw. 'Host' is kept literal, because the commentators differ on what it contains (living things, luminaries, angels).

Hebrew
בְּהַשָּׂגַת הַתַּכְלִית לַמְּצִיאוּת בִּכְלָלוֹ:
2:2

On the seventh day God finished his work that he had made, and on the seventh day he rested from all his work that he had made.

and-finished God on-the-day the-seventh work-his which he-made and-rested on-the-day the-seventh from-all-of work-his which he-made

Grammar
  • The verse repeats 'on the seventh day' and 'his work that he made' in two clauses: he finished, and he rested.
  • The etnaḥta after עָשָׂה divides the verse into the finishing and the resting.
  • וַיִּשְׁבֹּת is the verb from which 'Sabbath' comes; its sense is 'cease, desist', not 'be weary'.
  • אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה is a qatal inside a relative clause; the English pluperfect 'had made' shows that the work was done before.
  • The ב of בַּיּוֹם means 'on'. Some read it as 'before' (the work done before the seventh day); Ibn Ezra cites this view and rejects it: finishing a work is not doing work.

The English keeps 'On the seventh day' (Rashi's reading and the plain Hebrew). The view that the ב means 'before' (the work was finished before the seventh day) is cited by Ibn Ezra and rejected, and is recorded in the apparatus. The verbs finished and rested are not the same: 'finished' is Piel of כלה, 'rested' is Qal of שבת.

Commentary (11)
Rashinormativefollows וַיְכַ֤ל אֱלֹהִים֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔י
Rashi: God knows his times and moments exactly, so he entered the seventh day by a hair's breadth and it looked as though he finished in it; another reading: what was the world lacking? Rest; when Sabbath came, rest came, and the work was finished.
Hebrew
ר' שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר בָּשָׂר וָדָם, שֶׁאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ עִתָּיו וּרְגָעָיו צָרִיך לְהוֹסִיף מֵחֹל עַל הַקֹּדֶשׁ, הַקָּבָּ"ה שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ עִתָּיו וּרְגָעָיו, נִכְנָס בֹּו כְּחוּט הַשַּׂעֲרָה, וְנִרְאֶה כְאִלּוּ כִלָּה בוֹ בַיֹּום. דָּ"אַ מֶה הָיָה הָעוֹלָם חָסֵר? מְנוּחָה, בָּאת שַׁבָּת בָּאת מְנוּחָה, כָּלְתָה וְנִגְמְרָה הַמְּלָאכָה:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַיְכַ֤ל אֱלֹהִים֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔י
Ibn Ezra cites two views and rejects both: that the days were themselves created and the work was completed by the creation of the seventh day ("וזה הפירוש תפל"), and that the ב here means 'before', as in 'on the first day you shall remove leaven' (Ex 12:15). "ולמה זאת הצרה": the finishing of work is not work, as if it said he did no work on it; so too וַיְכַל and וַיִּשְׁבֹּת. The English keeps the plain 'on the seventh day'.

Apparatus
  • Rashi (R. Shimon): flesh and blood adds from the weekday to the holy day because he does not know his times; God does, so he finished exactly at the day's edge. Others, cited and rejected by Ibn Ezra: ב has the sense of 'before', as in Ex 12:15.
2:3 · פ

God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all his work that God created in order to make.

and-blessed God [object-marker] day-of the-seventh and-made-holy it because in-it he-rested from-all-of work-his which created God to-make

Grammar
  • וַיְבָרֶךְ and וַיְקַדֵּשׁ are two Piel wayyiqtols with the same subject; the second has the object marker with a suffix.
  • The etnaḥta on אֹתוֹ divides the verse before כִּי: the blessing and sanctifying, then the reason.
  • בּוֹ ('on it') is put before the verb for emphasis: on it, and not on another.
  • אֲשֶׁר־בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים לַעֲשׂוֹת: 'created ... to make' is hard; the infinitive may be final or may continue the verb 'created'.
  • The paragraph break (פ) after the verse closes the creation account's section on the seventh day.

The last clause is hard: the Hebrew has 'created to make'. The English keeps both verbs and the infinitive. Ibn Ezra takes it as creatures made with power to make their like; Rashi reads the 'making' as work that should have been done on the Sabbath and was doubled on the sixth day. The English follows Ibn Ezra's plain-sense reading and records Rashi's.

בְּשֵׁם ה' (בראשית ד':כ"ו), וְצָמַח צֶמַח צַדִּיק, כִּי מָשַׁךְ רַבִּים לָדַעַת אֶת ה', כְּמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ "וְאֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן" (שם יב ה), וְצִוָּה אֶת בֵּיתוֹ וְאֶת בָּנָיו אַחֲרָיו וְשָׁמְרוּ דֶּרֶךְ ה' לַעֲשׂוֹת צְדָקָה וּמִשְׁפָּט (יח יט), וְעָלָה הָעִנְיָן עַד שֶׁקִּבְּלוּ זַרְעוֹ אֶת הַתּוֹרָה בְּסִינַי וְנִבְנָה הַבַּיִת בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא, וְאָז נִתְקַיְּמוּ כָּל הַמִּצְוֹת שֶׁהֵם פֵּרוֹת הָעוֹלָם. וְדַע כִּי מֵעֵת הֱיוֹת בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת יֵחָשֵׁב כְּיוֹם מָחָר, וְעַל כֵּן יַתְחִיל עִנְיַן כָּל יוֹם קֹדֶם לוֹ מְעַט, כַּאֲשֶׁר נוֹלַד אַבְרָהָם בָּאֶלֶף הַשֵּׁנִי, וְכֵן תִּרְאֶה בְּכָל יוֹם וָיוֹם. וְהַיּוֹם הָרְבִיעִי נִבְרְאוּ בּוֹ הַמְּאוֹרוֹת הַגָּדוֹל וְהַקָּטָן וְהַכּוֹכָבִים, יוֹמוֹ יִרְמֹז בָּאֶלֶף הָד', הוּא הֵחֵל כַּאֲשֶׁר נִבְנָה בַּיִת רִאשׁוֹן ע"ב שָׁנָה אַחֲרֵי בִּנְיָנוֹ עַד אַחֲרֵי הַבַּיִת הַשֵּׁנִי קע"ב שָׁנָה. וְהִנֵּה בַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה לְכָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הָיָה אוֹר, כִּי מָלֵא כְבוֹד ה' אֶת בֵּית ה', וְהָיָה אוֹר יִשְׂרָאֵל לְאֵשׁ עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ רָבוּץ שָׁם כַּאֲרִי אוֹכֵל הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת, וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן הִקְטִין אוֹרָם וְגָלוּ כַּאֲשֶׁר יֵעָדֵר בְּמוֹלַד הַלְּבָנָה, וְזָרְחָה לָהֶם כָּל יְמֵי בַּיִת שֵׁנִי, וְהָאֵשׁ עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ רָבוּץ כְּכֶלֶב, וְשָׁקְעוּ שְׁנֵי הַמְּאוֹרִים בְּעֶרֶב הַיּוֹם וְחָרַב הַבַּיִת. בַּיּוֹם הַחֲמִישִׁי שָׁרְצוּ הַמַּיִם נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה וְעוֹף יְעוֹפֵף עַל הָאָרֶץ, רֶמֶז לָאֶלֶף הַחֲמִישִׁי הַמַּתְחִיל קע"ב שָׁנָה אַחַר חֻרְבַּן הַבַּיִת, כִּי בּוֹ יִמְשְׁלוּ הָאֻמּוֹת וְיֵעָשֶׂה אָדָם כִּדְגֵי הַיָּם כְּרֶמֶשׂ לֹא מֹשֵׁל בּוֹ, כֻּלּוֹ בְּחַכָּה הֵעֲלָה, יְגֹרֵהוּ בְחֶרְמוֹ וְיַאַסְפֵהוּ בְּמִכְמַרְתּוֹ, וְאֵין דּוֹרֵשׁ אֶת ה'. בַּיּוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי בַּבֹּקֶר "תּוֹצֵא הָאָרֶץ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה לְמִינָהּ בְּהֵמָה וָרֶמֶשׂ וְחַיְתוֹ אֶרֶץ לְמִינָהּ", וְהָיְתָה בְּרִיאָתָהּ קֹדֶם זְרֹחַ הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁכָּתוּב (תהלים קד כב) "תִּזְרַח הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ יֵאָסֵפוּן וְאֶל מְעוֹנֹתָם יִרְבָּצוּן", וְאָז נִבְרָא הָאָדָם בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים, וְהוּא זְמַן מֶמְשַׁלְתּוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שם כג) "יֵצֵא אָדָם לְפָעֳלוֹ וְלַעֲבֹדָתוֹ עֲדֵי עָרֶב", וְהוּא הָאֶלֶף הַשִּׁשִּׁי, כִּי בִּתְחִלָּתוֹ יִמְשְׁלוּ בּוֹ הַחַיּוֹת, הֵם הַמַּלְכִיּוֹת אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדְעוּ אֶת ה', וְאַחֲרֵי עֲשִׂירִיתוֹ כְּשִׁעוּר הָנֵץ הַחַמָּה לַיּוֹם (עיין פסחים צד) יָבֹא הַגּוֹאֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ (תהלים פט לז) "וְכִסְאוֹ כַּשֶּׁמֶשׁ נֶגְדִּי", זֶהוּ בֶּן דָּוִד הַנַּעֲשֶׂה בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים, כְּדִכְתִיב (דניאל ז':י"ג-י"ד) "וַאֲרוּ עִם עֲנָנֵי שְׁמַיָּא כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ אָתֵה הֲוָה וְעַד עַתִּיק יוֹמַיָּא מְטָה וּקְדָמוֹהִי הַקְרְבוּהִי וְלֵהּ יְהִיב שָׁלְטָן וִיקָר וּמַלְכוּ", וְיִהְיֶה זֶה קי"ח אַחַר חֲמֵשֶׁת אֲלָפִים לִכְלוֹת דְּבַר ה' מִפִּי דָּנִיֵּאל (שם יב יא) "וּמֵעֵת הוּסַר הַתָּמִיד וְלָתֵת שִׁקּוּץ שֹׁמֵם יָמִים אֶלֶף מָאתַיִם וְתִשְׁעִים". וְנִרְאֶה מִשִּׁנּוּי הַיָּמִים מִשֶּׁרֶץ הַמַּיִם וְהָעוֹף לְחַיַּת הָאָרֶץ, כִּי בִּתְחִלַּת הָאֶלֶף הַשִּׁשִּׁי תִּתְחַדֵּשׁ מַלְכוּת אֻמָּה שַׁלֶּטֶת וְאֵימְתָנִי וְתַקִּיפָא יַתִּירָא, וּמִתְקָרֶבֶת אֶל הָאֱמֶת יוֹתֵר מִן הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת. הַיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי שַׁבָּת, רֶמֶז לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ שַׁבָּת וּמְנוּחָה לְחַיֵּי הָעוֹלָמִים. וְהָאֵל יִשְׁמְרֵנוּ בְּכָל הַיָּמִים, כֵן
2:4

These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, on the day the LORD God made earth and heavens.

these generations-of the-heavens and-the-earth in-their-being-created in-day-of making LORD God earth and-heavens

Grammar
  • אֵלֶּה points back: Rashi, 'those mentioned above'; Ibn Ezra, 'these are what they begot'. The verse sums up the account of 1:1–2:3 and leads into what follows. It is the first place where the divine name יְהוָה appears, joined to אֱלֹהִים.
  • The etnaḥta after בְּהִבָּרְאָם divides the verse: the heavens and earth when created, and the day of the LORD God's making.
  • בְּהִבָּרְאָם is a Niphal infinitive construct with a pronominal suffix; בְּיוֹם עֲשׂוֹת is a construct before an infinitive.
  • The order 'the heavens and the earth' becomes 'earth and heavens' in the last words: a chiasm.
  • תּוֹלְדוֹת normally means offspring or the account of descendants.

'Generations' is kept literal (Ibn Ezra: these are what they begot). 'Made' renders עֲשׂוֹת; Ibn Ezra takes it as 'prepared, set in order', and the English 'made' leaves that room. The doubled name 'the LORD God' follows decisions.md.

2:5

No tree of the field was yet on the earth, and no plant of the field had yet sprung up, for the LORD God had not sent rain on the earth, and there was no human to work the ground.

and-all-of shrub-of the-field not-yet it-was in-the-earth and-all-of plant-of the-field not-yet it-sprouted for not he-sent-rain LORD God on the-earth and-human there-is-not to-work [object-marker] the-ground

Grammar
  • The verse is a series of negatives: no tree, no plant, no rain, no human.
  • טֶרֶם with the imperfect means 'not yet'; the English past perfect 'had yet sprung up' gives the sense.
  • The first pair uses יִהְיֶה and יִצְמָח, the reason clause uses a qatal (הִמְטִיר) in the Hiphil.
  • וְאָדָם אַיִן is a verbless clause, with אַיִן 'there is not' and the infinitive לַעֲבֹד 'to work'.
  • The etnaḥta after יִצְמָח separates the two statements from the reasons.
  • הָאֲדָמָה is the cultivated ground, and אָדָם is the one made from it: a pun that the English cannot keep.

'Tree' follows Ibn Ezra (and the Aramaic אילני); 'bush' or 'shrub' is the lexicon sense and is recorded. Rashi: 'not yet' (עד לא) is the meaning of טרם. The 'for' clause (no rain because no human to work the ground) is kept as the Hebrew has it; Rashi's explanation of why is recorded.

Grammar
  • יַעֲלֶה is a yiqtol after its subject, in a past setting. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as a past event: one rising of the mist before the human was formed. A yiqtol with a following weqatal can also describe repeated action ('a mist would rise and water').
  • וְהִשְׁקָה is a weqatal: a perfect with waw that continues the yiqtol before it.
  • The etnaḥta after הָאָרֶץ separates the rising from the watering.
  • The subject of וְהִשְׁקָה is 'the mist' (it watered); some read God as the one who waters.
  • אֵד is rare; here 'mist' is the sense given by Onkelos (cloud) and Ibn Ezra (smoke-like vapour).

The opening waw is read as 'but' because it sets the mist against the negatives of 2:5. 'Rose ... and watered' follows Rashi, who reads one act preparing the dust for the forming of the human (2:7), and Ibn Ezra's past paraphrase; the yiqtol and weqatal also allow a repeated action ('would rise and water'), recorded here. Saadia's view (that the clause says 'no mist rose') is recorded in Ibn Ezra's comment and not adopted. The subject of 'watered' is the mist.

Commentary (4)
Rashinormativefollows וְאֵ֖ד יַֽעֲלֶ֣ה
Rashi: this concerns the creation of the human. He brought up the deep and watered the clouds to soak the dust, and the human was created, like a kneader who puts in water and then kneads the dough: so here, first 'and watered', then 'and formed' (2:7).

Grammar
  • וַיִּיצֶר is a Qal wayyiqtol of a yod-initial verb; Rashi reads its two yods as two formings.
  • עָפָר מִן־הָאֲדָמָה: 'dust from the ground' may be in apposition to 'the human' or may be the material of forming.
  • בְּאַפָּיו is dual and means 'in his nostrils'; Ibn Ezra: through them a person lives.
  • וַיְהִי ... לְנֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה: 'became to a living being' uses ל to mark what he became.
  • A word-play: הָאָדָם 'the human' is made from הָאֲדָמָה 'the ground'.
  • The accents: the geresh on אֱלֹהִים closes the subject, the revia on הָאָדָם closes the object, the zaqef on הָאֲדָמָה ends the material; the etnaḥta after חַיִּים divides the forming and the breathing from the becoming.

'The human' with the article follows decisions.md. 'Living being' is the lexicon sense of נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה; Rashi notes that animals are also called this, and that the human's is the liveliest, because he has knowledge and speech. Ibn Ezra adds that he could walk at once, like animals, not like infants.

Commentary (19)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וַיִּ֩יצֶר֩
Rashi: two formings (two yods): one for this world and one for the resurrection; an animal, which is not subject to judgement, has no double yod. A homily on the spelling.

שְׁתֵּי יְצִירוֹת, יְצִירָה לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וִיצִירָה לִתְחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים, אֲבָל בַּבְּהֵמָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ עוֹמֶדֶת לַדִּין לֹא נִכְתַּב בִּיצִירָתָהּ שְׁנֵי יוֹדִי"ן:

2:8

The LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and put there the human whom he had formed.

and-planted LORD God garden in-Eden from-east and-put there [object-marker] the-human whom he-formed

Grammar
  • וַיִּטַּע and וַיָּשֶׂם are two wayyiqtols, 'planted' and 'put', with the same subject.
  • מִקֶּדֶם: 'from the east' or 'from of old'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as a place, 'in the east of Eden'; Onkelos (מִלְּקַדְמִין) and Ramban read it as time.
  • אֲשֶׁר יָצָר refers back to וַיִּיצֶר in 2:7.
  • The etnaḥta after מִקֶּדֶם divides the planting from the placing of the human.
  • גַּן־בְּעֵדֶן is bound by the maqqef: 'a garden-in-Eden'.

'In the east' follows Rashi and Radak; Onkelos and Genesis Rabbah read 'of old', and this is recorded. The relative clause 'whom he had formed' looks back to 2:7. The article on הָאָדָם is kept ('the human'); Ibn Ezra says it holds a secret.

Commentary (18)
Rashinormativefollows מִקֶּ֑דֶם
Rashi: in the east of Eden he planted the garden. The general-then-particular rule (Rabbi Eliezer son of Yose the Galilean): 'he created the human' is the general; 'and the LORD God formed' ... is the particular of the first.
Hebrew
בְּמִזְרָחוֹ שֶׁל עֵדֶן נָטַע אֶת הַגָּן. וְאִם תֹּאמַר, הֲרֵי כְבָר כָּתַב וַיִּבְרְָא אֶת הָאָדָם וְגוֹ', רָאִיתִי בִּבְרַיְתָא שֶׁל ר"א בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַ' יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי מל"ב מִדּוֹת שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה נִדְרֶשֶׁת, וְזוֹ אַחַת מֵהֶן, כְּלָל שֶׁלְּאַחֲרָיו מַעֲשֶׂה הוּא פְרָטוֹ שֶׁל רִאשׁוֹן, וַיִּבְרָא אֶת הָאָדָם זֶהוּ כְּלָל, סָתַם בְּרִיאָתוֹ מֵהֵיכָן וְסָתַם מַעֲשָׂיו, חָזַר וּפֵרֵשׁ וַיִּיצֶר ה' אֱלֹהִים וְגוֹ', וַיַּצְמַח לוֹ גַּן עֵדֶן וַיַּנִּיחֵהוּ בְּגַן עֵדֶן וַיַּפֵּל עָלָיו תַּרְדֵּמָה, הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ סָבוּר שֶׁהוּא מַעֲשֶׂה אַחֵר, וְאֵינוֹ אֶלָּא פְרָטוֹ שֶׁל רִאשׁוֹן; וְכֵן אֵצֶל הַבְּהֵמָה חָזַר וְכָתַב וַיִּצֶר ה' וגו' מִן הָאֲדָמָה כָּל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה, כְּדֵי לְפָרֵשׁ וַיָּבֵא אֶל הָאָדָם לִקְרוֹת שֵׁם וּלְלַמֵּד עַל הָעוֹפוֹת שֶׁנִּבְרְאוּ מִן הָרְקָק:

Ibn Ezra: the ה of הָאָדָם has a secret; also found in 'the Manasseh tribe', 'the Araunah, the Jebusite'; or it may be because the word is both a proper name and a description.
Hebrew
וה"א "האדם" יש לו סוד", גם נמצא "שבט המנשה" (דבר' ג יג), "הארוני, היבוסי", (ש"ב כד טז) וגם יתכן להיותו כן, בעבור שהוא שם נחצב מהאדמה והוא יהיה שם עצם ושם תואר:
Rambanrecords וַיִּטַּ֞ע יְהֹוָ֧ה אֱלֹהִ֛ים גַּן בְּעֵ֖דֶן מִקֶּ֑דֶם
Ramban: Rashi explains 'in the east of Eden'; Onkelos renders 'of old' (מִלְּקַדְמִין), as Genesis Rabbah says, "וְהוּא הַנָּכוֹן": that is the correct reading. 'Planted' does not mean the trees were brought from elsewhere; it marks them as the LORD's own planting, set out in order as a garden and lasting for ever.
Hebrew
פֵּרֵשׁ רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית ב':ח') בְּמִזְרָחוֹ שֶׁל עֵדֶן נָטַע הַגַּן. וְאוּנְקְלוֹס (תרגום אונקלוס על בראשית ב':ח') תִּרְגֵּם מִלְּקַדְמִין, וְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (בראשית רבה ט"ו:ג'), וְהוּא הַנָּכוֹן. וְאֵין טַעַם "וַיִּטַּע" שֶׁהֵבִיא הָאִילָנוֹת מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר וּנְטָעָן שָׁם, כִּי מִן הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא הִצְמִיחָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וַיַּצְמַח ה' אֱלֹהִים" וְגוֹ', אֲבָל עִנְיַן "וַיִּטַּע ה' אֱלֹהִים" לְהַגִּיד שֶׁהָיוּ מַטַּע ה', כִּי טֶרֶם שֶׁגָּזַר עַל הָאָרֶץ "תַּדְשֵׁא הָאָרֶץ דֶּשֶׁא" גָּזַר בַּמָּקוֹם הַהוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה שָׁם גַּן, וְאָמַר "בְּכָאן יִהְיֶה אִילָן פְּלוֹנִי וּבְכָאן אִילָן פְּלוֹנִי" כַּעֲרוּגַת הַמַּטָּעִים, וְלֹא הָיָה כְּדֶרֶךְ שְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת הָאָרֶץ שֶׁאָמַר "תַּדְשֵׁא הָאָרֶץ דֶּשֶׁא וְעֵץ פְּרִי", וְהִצְמִיחָה בְּלֹא סֵדֶר. וְהִנֵּה אִילָנֵי גַּן עֵדֶן גָּזַר בָּהֶם לַעֲשׂוֹת עָנָף וְלָשֵׂאת פֶּרִי לָעַד לְעוֹלָם, לֹא יַזְקִין בָּאָרֶץ שָׁרְשָׁם וּבֶעָפָר לֹא יָמוּת גִּזְעָם, אֵין צְרִיכִין לְעוֹבֵד וְזוֹמֵר, שֶׁאִלּוּ הָיוּ צְרִיכִין עֲבוֹדָה, אַחֲרֵי שֶׁגֹּרַשׁ הָאָדָם מִשָּׁם מִי עָבַד אוֹתָם. גַּם זֶה טַעַם "וַיִּטַּע ה' אֱלֹהִים", שֶׁהָיוּ מַטָּעָיו מַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו וְקַיָּמִים לְעוֹלָמִים, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (יחזקאל מז יב) "לֹא יִבּוֹל עָלֵהוּ וְלֹא יִתֹּם פִּרְיוֹ וְכוּ' כִּי מֵימָיו מִן הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הֵמָּה יוֹצְאִים". אִם כֵּן מָה טַעַם "וַיַּנִּחֵהוּ בְגַן עֵדֶן לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ" (בראשית ב':ט"ו) שֶׁהִנִּיחוֹ שָׁם לִהְיוֹת זוֹרֵעַ לוֹ חִטִּים וּמִינֵי תְּבוּאוֹת וְכָל עֵשֶׂב זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע וַעֲרוּגוֹת הַבְּשָׂמִים, וְקוֹצֵר וְתוֹלֵשׁ וְאוֹכֵל כִּרְצוֹנוֹ, וְזֶה טַעַם "לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ", לַעֲבֹד אַדְמַת הַגַּן הָעֲרוּגוֹת שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה שָׁם, כִּי הַגַּן שֶׁהֵם הָאִילָנוֹת לֹא יֵעָבְדוּ. וְיִתָּכֵן שֶׁכִּנָּה הַגַּן בִּלְשׁוֹן נְקֵבָה, כְּמוֹ "וּכְגַנָּה זֵרוּעֶיהָ תַצְמִיחַ" (ישעיהו סא יא), "וְנִטְעוּ גַנּוֹת" (ירמיהו כט ה). וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ נִתְעוֹרְרוּ בָּזֶה, אָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (בראשית רבה ט"ז:ה'), "לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ", אֵלּוּ הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שמות ג יב) "תַּעַבְדוּן אֶת הָאֱלֹהִים", הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב (במדבר כח ב), "תִּשְׁמְרוּ לְהַקְרִיב לִי בְּמוֹעֲדוֹ". וְהַכַּוָּנָה לָהֶם בָּזֶה לוֹמַר כִּי הַצְּמָחִים וְכָל בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים צְרִיכִים לַכּוֹחוֹת הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת, וּמֵהֶם יָבֹא לָהֶם הַגִּדּוּל, וּבַקָּרְבָּנוֹת יִהְיֶה מֶשֶׁךְ הַבְּרָכָה לָעֶלְיוֹנִים, וּמֵהֶם לְצִמְחֵי גַּן עֵדֶן, וּמֵהֶם יִהְיוּ וְיִחְיוּ לְעוֹלָם בְּגִשְׁמֵי רָצוֹן וּבְרָכָה שֶׁיִּגְדְּלוּ בָּהּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (ב"ר טו א), "יִשְׂבְּעוּ עֲצֵי ה' אַרְזֵי לְבָנוֹן אֲשֶׁר נָטָע" (תהלים קד טז), אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא, יִשְׂבְּעוּ חַיֵּיהֶן, יִשְׂבְּעוּ מֵימֵיהֶן, יִשְׂבְּעוּ מַטַּעְתָּן. כִּי "חַיֵּיהֶן" יְסוֹדוֹתָם הָעֶלְיוֹנִים, וּ"מֵימֵיהֶם" אוֹצָרוֹ הַטּוֹב הַמּוֹרִיד הַגֶּשֶׁם, וּ"מַטַּעְתָּן" כֹּחָם בַּשָּׁמַיִם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (ב"ר י ו), אֵין לְךָ כָּל עֵשֶׂב וְעֵשֶׂב מִלְּמַטָּה שֶׁאֵין לוֹ מַזָּל בָּרָקִיעַ וְהוּא מַכֶּה אוֹתוֹ וְאוֹמֵר לוֹ גְּדַל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (איוב לח לג), "הֲיָדַעְתָּ חֻקּוֹת שָׁמָיִם אִם תָּשִׂים מִשְׁטָרוֹ בָאָרֶץ", שׁוֹטֵר:
Radakfollows וַיִּטַּ֞ע
Radak: וַיִּטַּע means he brought it into existence there on the third day.
Hebrew
כְּמוֹ ״אַרְזֵי לְבָנוֹן אֲשֶׁר נָטָע״ (תהלים קד:טז), כְּלוֹמַר הִמְצִיאוֹ שָׁם בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי, וְזָכַר הַשֵּׁם עַל מְצִיאוּתוֹ לְפִי חֲשִׁיבוּתוֹ וּגְדֻלָּתוֹ, מַה שֶּׁלֹּא זָכַר בּוֹ בִּשְׁאָר הַצְּמָחִים בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי.

Apparatus
  • בְּעֵ֖דֶן — WLC reads בְעֵ֖דֶן (vowels)
2:9

The LORD God made grow from the ground every tree desirable to look at and good for food, and the tree of life in the middle of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

and-made-grow the-LORD God from-the-ground every-of tree desirable for-sight and-good for-food and-tree-of the-life in-midst-of the-garden and-tree-of the-knowledge good and-evil

Grammar
  • וַיַּצְמַח is a wayyiqtol Hiphil: the LORD God is the cause of the growth.
  • נֶחְמָד is a Niphal participle: 'desirable' (literally 'being desired'); it and טוֹב are both adjectival predicates of עֵץ.
  • The etnaḥta on לְמַאֲכָל ends the first half: all trees; the second half names the two special trees.
  • עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע: the Hebrew has no word between הַדַּעַת and טוֹב. The construct chain is elliptical, 'tree of the knowledge (of) good and evil'.
  • Ibn Ezra's reading: the text means 'the tree of the knowledge, the knowledge of good and evil' (he compares הָאָרוֹן הַבְּרִית), which is how the English line is built.

בְּתוֹךְ is rendered 'in the middle of' with Rashi and Radak (Targum Onkelos: בִּמְצִיעוּת גִּנְּתָא). Whether both trees stand at the one point or the middle is a broad area (Ramban) is left open by the Hebrew. 'Knowledge' stays a bare noun, 'of good and evil' being its content, following Ibn Ezra's supplied 'knowledge'.

2:10

A river flows out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divides and becomes four headwaters.

and-river going-out from-Eden to-water ACC the-garden and-from-there it-divides and-became into-four heads

Grammar
  • יֹצֵא is a participle with no auxiliary: the river is going out of Eden as a standing fact.
  • לְהַשְׁקוֹת is Hiphil: 'to cause to drink', hence 'to water'.
  • יִפָּרֵד is a Niphal yiqtol (it is divided, it splits). וְהָיָה is a weqatal, ו with the perfect, which continues the yiqtol with the same continuing sense: 'and becomes'.
  • רָאשִׁים is the plural of רֹאשׁ 'head'. The four 'heads' are named in the next verses.
  • The pashta on וּמִשָּׁם and the zaqef on יִפָּרֵד set 'from there it divides' as a unit.

רָאשִׁים is rendered 'headwaters': the 'heads' are the four beginnings of rivers (Radak: 'parts, since each part is the head of what comes out of it'). Whether the river first enters the garden and divides after leaving it (Radak) is not stated by the Hebrew. WLC vowels the first word with a dagesh in the resh; the base text here does not (see apparatus).

2:11

The name of the first is Pishon; it is the one that encircles the whole land of Havilah, where the gold is.

name-of the-one Pishon he the-encircling ACC all-of land-of the-Havilah which-there the-gold

Grammar
  • שֵׁם הָאֶחָד has no 'is': the verse is a nominal clause, 'the name of the first (river): Pishon'.
  • הוּא הַסֹּבֵב is a pronoun with an article-plus-participle: 'he, the encircler'.
  • אֲשֶׁר־שָׁם 'which-there' is the idiom for 'where'.
  • The revia on הַסֹּבֵב marks a pause before the object, and the zaqef on הַחֲוִילָה before the relative clause.
  • Each of the four names is introduced by שֵׁם and a number; the pattern runs from 2:11 to 2:14.

The English does not identify the river. Rashi says Pishon is the Nile of Egypt, named from its rising waters or from flax (פִּשְׁתָּן); Ibn Ezra reports the Gaon's identification as the Nile, doubts it from the geography, and says it is unproved. The Hebrew gives only name, circuit and the gold of Havilah. 'Encircle' for סבב fits Qal 2.d 'surround, encompass'.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativerecords פִּישׁ֑וֹן
Rashi: Pishon is the Nile, named for its waters rising and irrigating the land (cf. וּפָשׁוּ פָרָשָׁיו) or for flax (cf. עֹבְדֵי פִשְׁתִּים of Egypt); the identification and etymology are kept here, not in the English line.
Hebrew
הוּא נִילוּס נְהַר מִצְרַיִם, וְעַל שֵׁם שֶׁמֵּימָיו מִתְבָּרְכִין וְעוֹלִין וּמַשְׁקִין אֶת הָאָרֶץ נִקְרָא פִישׁוֹן כְּמוֹ וּפָשׁוּ פָּרָשָׁיו (חבקוק א') דָּ"אַ פִּישׁוֹן, שֶׁהוּא מְגַדֵּל פִּשְׁתָּן, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר עַל מִצְרַיִם (ישעיהו י"ט) וּבֹשׁוּ עֹבְדֵי פִשְׁתִּים:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows שֵׁ֥ם הָֽאֶחָ֖ד
Ibn Ezra: the Gaon said Pishon is the river of Egypt (the Nile). Ibn Ezra sets out the geography: Gihon is near the land of Israel, the Euphrates and Tigris are eastern, the Nile rises far south of the equator, and Eden lies under the equator. Pishon would then have to run south-west and turn back north. There is no proof that Pishon is the Nile: the Gaon rendered Havilah as he needed, without a tradition. The gold is mentioned in honour of the river that comes out of the garden.
Hebrew

Rambanrecords אֶ֣רֶץ הַֽחֲוִילָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר שָׁ֖ם הַזָּהָֽב׃
Ramban: 'where the gold is' shows that this is not the Havilah of Egypt (25:18), for this one is in the farthest east. Bdellium and onyx are named in praise of the river, since such gold and gems are found in the sand of rivers. On the earlier view (Rashi, Saadia), Pishon is the Nile, which encircles this Havilah and then runs through Egypt to the sea at Alexandria.

2:12

The gold of that land is good; bdellium is there, and onyx stone.

and-gold-of the-land the-that good there the-bdellium and-stone-of the-onyx

Grammar
  • הַהִוא is the feminine 'that', agreeing with הָאָרֶץ. In the Torah the feminine pronoun is regularly written הִוא and read hi.
  • Both clauses are nominal: no 'is'. The etnaḥta falls after טוֹב.
  • שָׁם before the noun puts weight on the place: 'there is the bdellium'.
  • וְאֶבֶן הַשֹּׁהַם is a construct chain, 'the stone of the onyx', while בְּדֹלַח has no 'stone' (Radak: it is too small to work).
  • The articles on הַבְּדֹלַח and הַשֹּׁהַם present them as the known goods of that land.

בְּדֹלַח and שֹׁהַם are of uncertain identity. Ibn Ezra and Radak take bdellium as a small round white stone (Num 11:7) and onyx as a fine white stone; the conventional 'bdellium' and 'onyx' are kept, and the other identifications are recorded here. The BDB entry for זָהָב offers only sense 10, which does not fit; the plain sense 'gold' is used. WLC vowels the first word with a hataf patah; the base text has a shewa.

2:13

The name of the second river is Gihon; it is the one that encircles the whole land of Cush.

and-name-of the-river the-second Gihon he the-encircling ACC all-of land-of Cush

Grammar
  • The verse is a copy of 2:11 in form: name, number, 'he the encircling'.
  • הוּא הַסּוֹבֵב is pronoun plus article and participle, 'he who encircles'.
  • The etnaḥta on גִּיחוֹן divides the name from the description. The zaqef qaton on הַסּוֹבֵב marks the pause before the object, and the silluq on כּוּשׁ closes the verse.
  • Radak notes that the river does not go from one side to the others: the land itself is what is encircled.
  • Rashi explains גִּיחוֹן by its great roaring, comparing כִּי יִגַּח (Ex 21:28, 'gores'). Radak takes it from גיח 'burst forth' (Job 40:23), because it sends out many branches.

The name receives its meaning in Rashi (surging, roaring, from גִּיחַ) and in Radak (a river that sends out many branches); neither belongs in the English line. 'Cush' is kept as a plain transliteration. The text does not say where Cush lies; Radak puts it in the south.

2:14

The name of the third river is the Tigris; it is the one that flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.

and-name-of the-river the-third Hiddekel he the-going east-of Asshur and-the-river the-fourth he Perat

Grammar
  • The third river has the same frame as 2:11 and 2:13; the fourth has no 'name of', only 'the fourth river, it is Perat'.
  • קִדְמַת is the construct of קִדְמָה, 'east'; Ibn Ezra reads the ת as the sign of a construct standing for the directive ה, 'to the east of Asshur'.
  • הַהֹלֵךְ is a participle with article: 'the one that goes'.
  • פְרָת has no 'name of' and no gloss because the river was well known, nearest to the land of Israel (Radak).
  • Rashi says Cush and Asshur 'did not yet exist': the text writes by the names of the future.

'Tigris' is the familiar English form of חִדֶּקֶל (Hiddekel); 'Euphrates' of פְּרָת (Perat); 'Assyria' of אַשּׁוּר. The meaning of each name goes in the notes, not in the English line (per decisions). The simple clause 'east of Assyria' follows Rashi and Ibn Ezra: toward the east of it, not 'in front of'.

Radak cites the Rabbis (Genesis Rabbah 16): R. Yehudah says Perat is the same river as Kevar (Ezekiel's Chebar), named for its fruitful and increasing waters, and Rav Huna says Perat and Kevar are separate rivers. Perat is not tied to any land because it is known on the border of the land of Israel. The four rivers mark the four quarters, and the account shows that Moses wrote by the holy spirit.

2:15

The LORD God took the human and set him in the garden of Eden to work it and guard it.

and-took the-LORD God ACC the-human and-set-him in-garden-of Eden to-work-it and-to-guard-it

Grammar
  • וַיַּנִּחֵהוּ is Hiphil of נוח with a pronominal suffix. The doubled נ marks the Hiphil הִנִּיחַ 'set down, place', not הֵנִיחַ 'give rest': 'and he set him'. It is a different verb from וַיָּשֶׂם in 2:8.
  • The feminine suffixes in לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ point to the garden, since גַּן may be feminine (Ibn Ezra); Radak also allows that they point to the ground.
  • The tevir on וַיִּקַּח and the etnaḥta on הָאָדָם divide the verse into 'took the human' and 'put him in the garden'.
  • Two infinitives with ל state purpose: 'to work it and to guard it'.
  • The wayyiqtol chain: took, set. The first repeats the 'put' of 2:8, adding purpose (Radak).

The suffix of לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ is feminine; Ibn Ezra takes it to refer to the garden (גַּן being of either gender), against those who refer it to הָאֲדָמָה (the ground), and so the English says 'it'. Ibn Ezra reads 'work' as watering the garden and 'guard' as keeping animals out; the English keeps the wider verbs 'work' and 'guard'. Rashi's 'took him with pleasant words' is a homiletic reading.

2:16

The LORD God commanded the human, saying: "You may eat freely from every tree of the garden.

and-commanded the-LORD God upon the-human to-say from-every-of tree-of the-garden eating you-will-eat

Grammar
  • The infinitive absolute אָכֹל before the finite תֹּאכֵל strengthens it: 'you may eat freely'; Radak compares שָׁמוֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּן.
  • וַיְצַו עַל takes עַל before the person: the idiom opens a command, here a restriction (Ibn Ezra).
  • The object מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן is fronted, putting the permission first. The imperfect is permissive: 'you may'.
  • The etnaḥta on לֵאמֹר separates the narrative from the speech.
  • Because the speech continues in 2:17, the sentence is only the first half of the command.

The imperfect with infinitive absolute is rendered as a permission with 'freely' (Radak: the infinitive strengthens the verb). Ibn Ezra reads צִוָּה עַל as introducing the prohibition of 2:17: although the fruit of the garden is allowed, the tree of knowledge is not. Radak asks whether the command refers to 'you shall not eat' or to both parts. The speech runs on into 2:17, so the quotation is left open here.

2:17

But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you must not eat from it, for on the day you eat from it you will surely die.

and-from-tree-of the-knowledge-of good and-evil not you-will-eat from-it for in-day-of your-eating from-it die-INFABS you-will-die

Grammar
  • The object is fronted: 'and from the tree ... not you shall eat from it'. The same tree is named with a repeated pronoun, וּמֵעֵץ ... מִמֶּנּוּ.
  • לֹא תֹאכַל is an imperfect with 'not', a prohibition (compare 'you must not'), in contrast to the permission of 2:16.
  • בְּיוֹם אֲכׇלְךָ is a temporal clause built on a construct noun and an infinitive construct with a suffix.
  • מוֹת תָּמוּת joins the infinitive absolute to the finite verb for certainty ('you will surely die'). The etnaḥta falls on מִמֶּנּוּ and divides prohibition from reason; silluq closes the verse.

The English keeps the order 'from the tree ... you must not eat from it', as the Hebrew fronts the object. 'Evil' is chosen for רָע (it is the noun here, paired with good). The sense of מוֹת תָּמוּת is left as 'surely die', without saying when death comes; Ramban and Radak read the day as the time at which one becomes liable to death.

Commentary (8)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: after saying 'from the tree' the word מִמֶּנּוּ is added to make it clear, like 'she opened it and saw him, the child' (Ex 2:6); or it means 'not even a little of it'. The man was full of knowledge, since he named the animals; only the knowledge of good and evil in one matter he lacked. The English keeps the double 'from the tree ... from it'.
Hebrew
ואחר שאמר מעץ הדעת לא תאכל, מה צורך למלת ממנו רק הוסיף לבאר, וכן "ותפתח ותראהו את הילד" (שמות ב ו), או טעמו אפילו מעט ממנו, ודקדוק "ממנו" בס' היסוד תמצאנו, ודע כי אדם מלא דעת היה כי השם לא יצוה לאשר אין לו דעת רק דעת טוב ורע בדבר אחד לבדו לא ידע הלא תראה שקרא שמות לכל הבהמה והעוף כפי תולדת כל אחד ואחד והנה חכם גדול היה, ולולי שהיה כן לא הביא השם את בריאותיו אליו לראות מה יקראם, והוא יודע ממנו שהוא בער, גם השם הראה לו עץ הדעת, כי הנה אשתו ידעה שהוא בתוך הגן:
Rambanrecords לֹ֥א תֹאכַ֖ל מִמֶּ֑נּוּ

מִן הַפְּרִי יַזְהִירֶנּוּ, כִּי הָעֵץ אֵינוֹ נֶאֱכָל. וְכֵן אָמַר לְמַטָּה (בראשית ג':ג') "מִפְּרִי הָעֵץ אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹךְ הַגָּן", וְכָמֹהוּ "וְאִכְלוּ אִישׁ גַּפְנוֹ וְאִישׁ תְּאֵנָתוֹ" (מלכים ב יח לא) וְכֵן "בְּעִצָּבוֹן תֹּאכֲלֶנָּה" (בראשית ג':י"ז) תֹּאכַל פִּרְיָהּ:
Rambanrecords בְּי֛וֹם אֲכׇלְךָ֥ מִמֶּ֖נּוּ מ֥וֹת תָּמֽוּת׃
Ramban: 'on the day you eat' means the time when one becomes liable to death, as in 1 Kings 2:42; it does not mean he dies within the day.
Hebrew
בְּעֵת שֶׁתֹּאכַל מִמֶּנּוּ תִּהְיֶה בֶּן מָוֶת, וְכָמוֹהוּ "בְּיוֹם צֵאתְךָ וְהָלַכְתָּ אָנֶה וָאָנָה יָדֹעַ תֵּדַע כִּי מוֹת תָּמוּת" (מלכים א ב מב), שֶׁאֵין הַכַּוָּנָה שֶׁיָּמוּת מִיָּד בּוֹ בַּיּוֹם, וְאֵין הַכַּוָּנָה לִידִיעָה בִּלְבַד שֶׁיֵּדַע שֶׁיָּמוּת, כִּי הַחַיִּים יוֹדְעִים שֶׁיָּמֻתוּ כֻּלָּם, אֲבָל הַכַּוָּנָה כִּי בְּעֵת שֶׁיֵּצֵא יִהְיֶה חַיָּב מִיתָה לַמֶּלֶךְ וְהוּא יָמִית אוֹתוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר יִרְצֶה. "וְלֹא יָבֹאוּ לִרְאוֹת כְּבַלַּע אֶת הַקֹּדֶשׁ וָמֵתוּ" (במדבר ד כ), "וְלֹא יִשְׂאוּ עָלָיו חֵטְא וּמֵתוּ בוֹ כִּי יְחַלְּלֻהוּ" (ויקרא כב ט), אֵין עִנְיָנָם אֶלָּא שֶׁיִּהְיוּ חַיָּבִים מִיתָה, וְיָמוּתוּ בְּחֶטְאָם זֶה. וְעַל דַּעַת אַנְשֵׁי הַטֶּבַע הָיָה הָאָדָם מְעֻתָּד לְמִיתָה מִתְּחִלַּת הַיְּצִירָה, מִפְּנֵי הֱיוֹתוֹ מֻרְכָּב, אֲבָל גָּזַר עַתָּה שֶׁאִם יֶחֱטָא יָמוּת בְּחֶטְאוֹ כְּדֶרֶךְ חַיָּבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם בַּעֲבֵרוֹת, כְּגוֹן זָר הָאוֹכֵל תְּרוּמָה (ויקרא כט ט) וּשְׁתוּי יַיִן (שם י ט) וּמְחֻסַּר בְּגָדִים שֶׁשִּׁמְּשׁוּ (שמות כח מג) וְזוּלָתָם, שֶׁהַכַּוָּנָה בָּהֶם שֶׁיָּמוּתוּ בְּחֶטְאָם טֶרֶם בֹּא יוֹמָם. וּלְכָךְ אָמַר בָּעֹנֶשׁ, "עַד שׁוּבְךָ אֶל הָאֲדָמָה כִּי מִמֶּנָּה לֻקָּחְתָּ כִּי עָפָר אַתָּה וְאֶל עָפָר תָּשׁוּב" בְּטִבְעֲךָ (בראשית ג':י"ט). וְגַם מִתְּחִלָּה הָיָה אוֹכֵל מִפְּרִי הָעֵץ וּמִזֶּרַע הָאָרֶץ, אִם כֵּן הָיְתָה בּוֹ הַתָּכָה וְסִבַּת הֲוָיָה וְהֶפְסֵד. וְעַל דַּעַת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (עיין שבת נה) אִלְמָלֵא שֶׁחָטָא לֹא מֵת לְעוֹלָם, כִּי הַנְּשָׁמָה הָעֶלְיוֹנִית נוֹתֶנֶת לוֹ חַיִּים לָעַד, וְהַחֵפֶץ הָאֱלֹהִי אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ בְּעֵת הַיְּצִירָה יִהְיֶה דָּבֵק בּוֹ תָּמִיד וְהוּא יְקַיֵּם אוֹתוֹ לָעַד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁפֵּרַשְׁתִּי בְּמִלַּת "וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים כִּי טוֹב" (לעיל א ד). וְדַע כִּי אֵין הַהַרְכָּבָה מוֹרָה עַל הַהֶפְסֵד אֶלָּא לְדַעַת קְטַנֵּי אֲמָנָה כִּי הַבְּרִיאָה הִיא בְּחִיּוּב, אֲבָל לְדַעַת אַנְשֵׁי הָאֱמוּנָה הָאוֹמְרִים כִּי הָעוֹלָם מְחֻדָּשׁ בְּחֵפֶץ אֱלֹהִי פָּשׁוּט, גַּם הַקִּיּוּם יִהְיֶה בּוֹ לָעַד כָּל יְמֵי הַחֵפֶץ, וְזֶה אֱמֶת בָּרוּר. אִם כֵּן "בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְךָ מִמֶּנּוּ מוֹת תָּמוּת", שֶׁאָז תִּהְיֶה בֶּן מָוֶת, לֹא תִּתְקַיֵּם לָעַד בְּחֶפְצִי, וְהָאֲכִילָה הָיְתָה לוֹ מִתְּחִלָּה לְעֹנֶג. וְיִתָּכֵן שֶׁפֵּרוֹת גַּן עֵדֶן נִבְלָעִים בָּאֵבָרִים כַּמָּן וּמְקַיְּמִים אֶת אוֹכְלֵיהֶם, וְכַאֲשֶׁר גָּזַר עָלָיו "וְאָכַלְתָּ אֶת עֵשֶׂב הַשָּׂדֶה" וּבְזֵעַת אַפָּיו יֹאכַל לֶחֶם הָאֲדָמָה, הָיָה זֶה סִבָּה לַהֶפְסֵד, כִּי עָפָר הוּא וְעָפָר יֹאכַל וְאֶל עָפָר יָשׁוּב:

Apparatus
  • The pack parses the suffix of מִמֶּנּוּ as 1st person plural; the form is the usual 3rd masc. sing. 'from it' with a doubled nun, and the English follows the sense.
2:18

The LORD God said, "It is not good for the human to be alone; I will make for him a helper corresponding to him."

and-said the-LORD God not good to-be the-human by-himself I-will-make for-him help like-opposite-him

Grammar
  • לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ: an infinitive construct with its own subject, הָאָדָם, after a predicate adjective.
  • אֶעֱשֶׂה־לּוֹ is a 1st person imperfect, here a resolve of the speaker ('I will make').
  • עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ is two words: 'a help' and 'like his counterpart'; כְּנֶגְדּוֹ is not a verb but a prepositional phrase.
  • The etnaḥta falls on לְבַדּוֹ and divides the statement from the resolve.

'Corresponding to him' keeps the meaning 'a match, what stands opposite him' (Sforno: as one equal to him; Radak: before him, always ready to help him). Rashi's reading, 'against him, to fight' if he is not worthy, is kept in the commentary entry.

Commentary (13)

Apparatus

2:19

The LORD God formed from the ground every animal of the field and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the human to see what he would call it. Whatever the human called each living creature, that was its name.

and-formed the-LORD God from-the-ground every-of animal-of the-field and-OBJ every-of bird-of the-heavens and-brought to-the-human to-see what he-would-call to-him and-every which he-would-call to-him the-human living soul that his-name

Grammar
  • וַיִּצֶר is a wayyiqtol of יצר (the yod of the root is dropped in writing, as Radak notes); the sequence continues the narrative but does not fix a new moment (compare 'had formed').
  • לִרְאוֹת מַה־יִּקְרָא־לוֹ: purpose, with an indirect question, 'to see what he would call it'.
  • וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָא־לוֹ הָאָדָם נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה הוּא שְׁמוֹ is a hard construction: 'and all which the human would call to it, a living being, that is its name'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra both read נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה as the thing named.
  • Wordplay: אֲדָמָה (ground), אָדָם (human).

For the last clause the English follows the agreed reading of Rashi and Ibn Ezra: 'each living creature the human called, that was its name'. Ramban gives a different reading (the human calls each kind 'a living being' like himself, and so finds none a help); it is kept in the commentary.

Commentary (18)
Rashinormativefollows וַיִּ֩צֶר֩ מִן הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה
Rashi: 'formed' is the same act as the 'making' of the beasts above; Scripture adds that birds were made from the ground (the swamp), and that they were brought to the human the same day to be named. In aggadah, 'form' means 'subdue'.

2:20

The human gave names to all the livestock and the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for himself the human did not find a helper corresponding to him.

and-called the-human names to-every-of the-livestock and-to-bird-of the-heavens and-to-every-of animal-of the-field and-for-human not he-found help like-opposite-him

Grammar
  • לְכָל־הַבְּהֵמָה: Ibn Ezra says the word לְכָל 'draws itself and another with it': its 'all' also governs וּלְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם, 'and to all the birds of the sky' (compare Deut 33:6, Prov 30:3).
  • Anarthrous וּלְאָדָם: Ibn Ezra reads 'and for himself', as the Hebrew idiom puts the name of a person for the person. Rashi has the human speak of himself.
  • The subject of לֹא־מָצָא is the human, not the LORD God (Ibn Ezra calls the reading with the LORD as subject 'far').
  • The zaqef gadol on וּלְאָדָם marks the turn from the naming to the lack.

'For himself' follows Ibn Ezra: the noun אָדָם, without the article, stands for the pronoun, and the human is the subject of מָצָא. Rashi agrees on the subject: the human says 'I have no mate'. 'All' is given to the livestock and the birds together, as Ibn Ezra reads לְכָל. A proper-name reading 'for Adam' is kept in the apparatus.

Commentary (6)
Rashinormativefollows וּלְאָדָ֕ם לֹֽא מָצָ֥א עֵ֖זֶר
Rashi: when each kind was brought, male and female, he said: all have a mate and I have none; at once, 'And the LORD God cast a deep sleep'.

ומלת לכל הבהמה, גם היא מושכת עצמה ואחרת עמה, כי טעמו ולכל עוף השמים, וכן "ויהי מתיו ממפר" (דבר' לג ו), וכן "ולא למדתי חכמה" (משלי ל, ג),, ורבים כאלה,

Ibn Ezra: 'and for the human he found none' means 'for himself he found none', as Hebrew idiom has it (1 Sam 12:11); he rejects the reading in which the LORD is the subject. Here he adds that the birds were formed from the ground, and above from the waters, since from both.

Rambanrecords וּלְאָדָ֕ם לֹֽא מָצָ֥א עֵ֖זֶר כְּנֶגְדּֽוֹ׃
Ramban praises Rashi's reading (the naming is placed inside the account of the helper). His own view: the naming was itself the search for a helper. In naming, the human set apart the kinds that can breed with one another, and found none fit for himself. 'For Adam' means 'for the name of Adam', a helper to be called by his name.

Grammar
  • הִפִּיל תַּרְדֵּמָה is a Hifil of נפל with an object: 'made a deep sleep fall' on the human; Ibn Ezra notes the 'heavy' stem.
  • וַיִּישַׁן, וַיִּקַּח, וַיִּסְגֹּר: a run of wayyiqtols narrates the operation.
  • אַחַת מִצַּלְעֹתָיו: the numeral is feminine to agree with צֵלָע; the partitive מִ gives 'one of his sides'.
  • תַּחְתֶּנָּה has a nun added to the feminine suffix (Radak, Ibn Ezra), as תַּחְתֶּיהָ.

Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that צֵלָע is 'side' here (Rashi: 'his sides', as in 'the side of the tabernacle'; Ibn Ezra: 'side'). The English follows: 'one of his sides'. 'Rib' (Targum Onkelos עלעא, Radak's second view) is kept in the apparatus.

Apparatus
  • 'Rib' (Onkelos, Radak's second view) is the common rendering of צֵלָע; the English follows Rashi and Ibn Ezra's 'side'.
2:22

The LORD God built the side that he had taken from the human into a woman, and brought her to the human.

and-built the-LORD God OBJ-the-side which he-took from-the-human to-woman and-brought-her to-the-human

Grammar
  • וַיִּבֶן is a shortened wayyiqtol of בנה in the Qal ('built'). Ibn Ezra says the form can be taken from the 'heavy' stem and also from the 'light' stem, like וַיִּפֶן and וַיִּקֶן. The verb takes the side as object.
  • לְאִשָּׁה: the preposition ל marks the result of the building, 'into a woman' (Rashi), not a purpose clause.
  • אֲשֶׁר־לָקַח is a perfect in a relative clause, a pluperfect in sense ('had taken').
  • From וַיִּבֶן the conjunctive accents (telisha qetana, qadma, darga) bind the verb to its subject. The paseq after אֱלֹהִים and the tevir on הַצֵּלָע make the first breaks, and the etnaḥta on לְאִשָּׁה divides the building from the bringing.

Rashi's 'built' as 'in the form of a building, wide below and narrow above' bears on the picture of the verb and is kept in the commentary entry; the English uses 'built' as the plain word.

2:23

Then the human said, "This one, this time, is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. This one shall be called woman, for from man this one was taken."

and-said the-human this the-time bone from-my-bones and-flesh from-my-flesh to-this-one it-will-be-called woman for from-man was-taken this-one

Grammar
  • זֹאת הַפַּעַם: 'this one, the time', hence 'this time'. The etnaḥta on מִבְּשָׂרִי divides the verse into the recognition and the naming. In the first half, the revia on הַפַּעַם and the zaqef on מֵעֲצָמַי set off 'this time', 'bone of my bones' and 'flesh of my flesh'.
  • עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי: two parallel lines, with a verbless clause: the first colon names bone, the second flesh.
  • אִשָּׁה and אִישׁ: a wordplay. Rashi: the Holy Tongue is the language of creation; Ibn Ezra explains the dagesh in שׁ as in place of the yod of אִישׁ.
  • יִקָּרֵא is a Nifal imperfect; לֻקְחָה is a Pual perfect (WLC vowels לֻקֳחָה). The qof has no dagesh (Radak: 'the qof is rafe').

'This time' is the plain sense; Rashi's homily (the human had come on every beast and was not satisfied) is not adopted. Radak: this time (not the first, when the animals were brought).

Apparatus
  • WLC reads לֻקֳחָה for MAM לֻקְחָה (vowels, 2:23.14); the same word.
  • לֻֽקְחָה — WLC reads לֻֽקֳחָה (vowels)
2:24

Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.

upon-so he-leaves man OBJ his-father and-OBJ his-mother and-clings to-his-wife and-they-become to-flesh one

Grammar
  • עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ: an imperfect after 'therefore' states a general rule, hence the present tense of the English.
  • וְדָבַק and וְהָיוּ are weqatal forms that continue the imperfect; the subject changes from 'a man' to 'they' (the man and his wife).
  • לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד: 'into one flesh', ל marking the result; compare Rashi and Ibn Ezra on the sense of unity.
  • The pashta on כֵּן and the zaqef on אִישׁ divide the verse; the etnaḥta falls on אִמּוֹ.

The tense is present because the verse states a rule that follows from what was just done. Rashi's homily about the prohibition of incest is a legal derivation and does not bear on the English. 'One flesh' is read, as Ibn Ezra reads it, as 'as if they were one'; Rashi's 'the child' and the sense of procreation are kept in the commentary entry.

2:25

The two of them were naked, the human and his wife, and they were not ashamed.

and-were two-of-them naked the-human and-his-wife and-not they-were-ashamed

Grammar
  • שְׁנֵיהֶם is the dual construct of שְׁנַיִם with a suffix, 'the two of them'; הָאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ then names the two in apposition.
  • עֲרוּמִּים 'naked' (the מ is doubled) is a different word from עָרוּם 'shrewd' in 3:1. The sound-play joins the two scenes; Ibn Ezra notes the pair at 3:1.
  • וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ is a yiqtol after a wayyiqtol: it describes a continuing state, 'and they were not ashamed', not a single event. The verb is a hitpolel (reflexive or reciprocal) of בוש; Ibn Ezra: from a root with a hidden quiet letter, the last letter doubled, as in יִתְבּוֹנָן (Job 11:11).
  • The etnaḥta on וְאִשְׁתּוֹ divides the verse after the naming of the two; the qamets of יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ is pausal, because the word ends the verse (Ibn Ezra).

'Ashamed' renders the hitpolel; the Hebrew does not say before whom (BDB: ashamed before one another). Rashi and Radak differ on the reason for the absence of shame (no knowledge of modesty and the evil inclination; no sexual desire yet); the English gives the fact, not the reason.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos: עַרְטִילָאִין 'naked' and לָא מִתְכַּלְמִין 'not ashamed'; the same sense as the Hebrew.
  • Sforno: their organs served God's will alone, so the act of union was like eating and drinking; this explains the absence of shame and does not change the words.
3:1

Now the serpent was shrewder than every wild animal that the LORD God had made. It said to the woman, “Is it really so that God said, ‘You must not eat from any tree of the garden’?”

and-the-serpent was shrewd than-all-of living-thing-of the-field which made the-LORD God and-said to-the-woman also that said God not you-eat from-all-of tree-of the-garden

Grammar
  • וְהַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם is waw + subject + qatal: a background clause that introduces a new character, not a step in the narrative sequence.
  • עָרוּם 'shrewd' and עֲרוּמִּים 'naked' (2:25) sound alike; Ibn Ezra takes this as deliberate play on the two senses, as in Judges 15:16 and 10:4. Radak distinguishes them by vowels: shureq for wisdom, holem for 'naked'.
  • מִכֹּל after the adjective is the comparative min: 'shrewder than all'. Rashi sets it beside 'cursed above all' (3:14).
  • אַף כִּי has no interrogative particle: the question is carried by the elliptical אַף כִּי and by tone. The serpent says אֱלֹהִים and not יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים, the name used by the narrator (Ibn Ezra: they did not know the name).
  • The etnaḥta on אֱלֹהִים (3:1.10) ends the narrator's description. The pashta on וַיֹּאמֶר is written twice because the word is stressed on its first syllable: pashta stands on the last letter, and a second sign marks the stressed syllable.

אַף כִּי is difficult. Ibn Ezra reads it as showing that other words came first and ending in an a fortiori ('how much more, that He said you may not eat from any tree'); Rashi reads 'perhaps He said you may not eat from any of them', an exaggeration meant to draw her answer. The English 'Is it really so that' keeps the question and the overstatement and drops 'even/also'. מִכֹּל עֵץ can mean 'from any tree at all' or 'from every tree'; the English keeps 'any'. The serpent is read as a real serpent that speaks (Ibn Ezra, Radak), not as a figure; Sforno's reading of it as the evil inclination is recorded in the apparatus.

Commentary (22)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וְהַנָּחָשׁ֙ הָיָ֣ה עָר֔וּם
Rashi: why is this here? It should follow with 'And He made garments of skin' (3:21); it teaches by what counsel the serpent leapt at them: he saw them naked and engaged in intercourse in public, and desired her. A homily on the link to 2:25; the English keeps the link with 'Now'.

Ibn Ezra rejects the views that the woman understood the speech of animals and the serpent spoke by hints, that the serpent was Satan, and Saadia's view that an angel spoke for it; he holds that the words are as they sound: the serpent spoke and walked upright. Ibn Ezra: אף כי shows that he said other words first and ended with an a fortiori: He said not to eat of any tree at all. The serpent did not use the divine name because they did not know it; the woman later added 'and you shall not touch it'.
Hebrew
וטעם אף כי יורה כי דבר דברים אחרים, ואמר בסוף קל וחומר שאמר לכם לא תאכלו פרי כל עץ כלל "לא הזכיר הנחש השם הנכבד והנורא כי לא ידעו, גם האשה הוסיפה על מצות השם, ולא תגעו בו, וכן הוסיפה אשת מנוח עד יום מותו (שופ' יג ז):
Radak וְהַנָּחָשׁ֙ הָיָ֣ה עָר֔וּם מִכֹּל֙ חַיַּ֣ת הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֖ה יְהֹוָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֑ים
Hebrew
יֵשׁ לִשְׁאֹל עַל עִנְיַן אֲמִירַת הַנָּחָשׁ לָאִשָּׁה אֵיךְ הָיָה, וְאִם הָיָה דֶּרֶךְ מוֹפֵת כְּמוֹ אֲמִירַת הָאָתוֹן לְבִלְעָם, לָמָּה לֹא אָמַר ״וַיִּפְתַּח ה׳ אֶת פִּי הַנָּחָשׁ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״וַיִּפְתַּח ה׳ אֶת פִּי הָאָתוֹן״ (במדבר כב:כח)? וְאִם כְּדִבְרֵי רַבִּי סַעַדְיָה שֶׁכָּתַב שֶׁלֹּא דִּבֵּר הַנָּחָשׁ וְלֹא הָאָתוֹן אֶלָּא מַלְאָךְ דִּבֵּר בַּעֲבוּרָם, לָמָּה נִתְקַלֵּל הַנָּחָשׁ? וְעוֹד אֵיךְ יַשִּׂיא הַמַּלְאָךְ אֶת הָאִשָּׁה לַעֲבֹר עַל מִצְוַת הָאֵל? וְעוֹד מַה עִנְיָן לַנָּחָשׁ הֵנָּה? וְלָמָּה אָמַר וְהַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם אַחַר שֶׁהוּא לֹא דִּבֵּר? וְאִם נֹאמַר כִּי לְנַסּוֹת אֶת הָאִשָּׁה בָּא הַמַּלְאָךְ אִם תַּעֲבֹר אֶת פִּי ה׳, מַה חֵטְא הַנָּחָשׁ בָּזֶה, וְלָמָּה לֹא בָּא הַמַּלְאָךְ לְאָדָם כִּי לֹא הָיְתָה מִצְוַת הָאֵל לָאִשָּׁה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָדָם אָמַר לָאִשָּׁה מִצְוַת הָאֵל? וְהָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה מְבֻלְבָּל מְאֹד לְפִי הַנִּגְלֶה אֲבָל לְפִי הַנִּסְתָּר הָעִנְיָן מְבֹאָר כְּמוֹ שֶׁנְּפָרֵשׁ בְּקוּנְדְרֵס אֲשֶׁר נִכְתֹּב לְבַדּוֹ בַּנִּסְתָּר. וּמֵהַנִּסְתָּר מַה שֶׁכָּתְבוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בָּזֶה (פרקי דרבי אליעזר יג) כִּי הַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה גָּדוֹל כְּגָמָל וְסָמָאֵל רוֹכֵב עָלָיו, וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שׂוֹחֵק עַל הַגָּמָל וְרוֹכְבוֹ, וְהָבֵן זֶה בָּזֶה, כִּי מַה מְּאֹד נִכְבָּד הַמָּשָׁל הַזֶּה בְּדִבְרֵיהֶם. וְעוֹד אָמְרוּ (יבמות קג ע״ב, עבודה זרה כב ע״ב) כְּשֶׁבָּא נָחָשׁ עַל חַוָּה הִטִּיל בָּהּ זוּהֲמָא, יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁעָמְדוּ עַל הַר סִינַי פָּסְקָה זוּהֲמָתָן, אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁלֹּא עָמְדוּ עַל הַר סִינַי לֹא פָּסְקָה זוּהֲמָתָן, וְכָל זֶה נָכוֹן לַמֵּבִין. וַאֲנַחְנוּ לֹא נְבָאֵר הֵנָּה הַמָּשָׁל שֶׁלֹּא נְגַלֶּה הַנִּסְתָּר כְּמוֹ שֶׁהִזְהִירוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עָלָיו כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְנוּ, אֲבָל נִכְתֹּב הָרְמִיזוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁרָמְזוּ הֵם, וְהַמֵּבִין יָבִין. וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים כִּי הַנָּחָשׁ לֹא דִּבֵּר, אֶלָּא בְּצִפְצוּף רָמַז לָאִשָּׁה, וְהָאִשָּׁה הִכִּירָה בִּרְמִיזַת הַנָּחָשׁ וְיָדְעָה כִּי זֶה רָצָה לוֹמַר. וְזֶה רָחוֹק שֶׁתָּבִין הָאִשָּׁה הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה בִּרְמִיזוֹת, וְעוֹד אִם הָאִשָּׁה הֵבִינָה רְמִיזוֹת הַנָּחָשׁ אֵיךְ הֵבִין מַעֲנֵה הָאִשָּׁה. וְהֶחָכָם רַבִּי אַבְרָהָם בֶּן עֶזְרָא כָּתַב כִּי הַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה מְדַבֵּר, וְהָיָה הוֹלֵךְ בְּקוֹמָה זְקוּפָה, וְהַשֵּׁם שָׂם בּוֹ דַּעַת הָאָדָם. וְהִנֵּה הַפָּסוּק הֵעִיד כִּי הָיָה
Radak עָר֔וּם מִכֹּל֙ חַיַּ֣ת הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה
Hebrew
רַק לֹא כָּאָדָם, וְכֵן דַּעַת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בראשית רבה כ:ה) וְיֵשׁ לִתְמֹהַּ לְפֵרוּשׁ הֶחָכָם הַזֶּה אֵיךְ בְּעֵת הַבְּרִיאָה לֹא הִבְדִּילוֹ מִן הַבְּהֵמוֹת וּמִן הַחַיּוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁהִבְדִּיל הָאָדָם שֶׁאָמַר עָלָיו ״נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ״ (בראשית א:כו)? וְעוֹד כַּאֲשֶׁר קִלֵּל הַנָּחָשׁ וְאָמַר לוֹ ״עַל גְּחֹנְךָ תֵלֵךְ וְעָפָר תֹּאכַל״ (בראשית ג:יד) אֵיךְ לֹא אָמַר ״וְדַעַת תֶּחְסַר״ כִּי הִיא הַקְּלָלָה הַגְּדוֹלָה וְאֵיךְ לֹא הִזְכִּירָהּ? וְהַקָּרוֹב בְּכָל מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְנוּ הוּא שֶׁהָיָה דִּבּוּר הַנָּחָשׁ עַל דֶּרֶךְ מוֹפֵת לְנַסּוֹת בּוֹ הָאִשָּׁה; וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא אָמַר ״וַיִּפְתַּח ה׳ אֶת פִּי הַנָּחָשׁ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר בַּאָתוֹן בִּלְעָם לְפִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּזֶה נִסְתָּר גָּדוֹל וְהוּא הָעִקָּר לִמְבִינֵי מַדָּע; וַעֲדַיִן יֵשׁ לִשְׁאֹל לָמָּה נִתְקַלֵּל הַנָּחָשׁ אַחַר שֶׁהָאֵל שָׂם הַדָּבָר בְּפִיו? וְיֵשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ כִּי הַנָּחָשׁ חָשַׁב בְּעַרְמִימוּת לְקַנֵּא בָּאָדָם, וְהָאֵל שֶׁיָּדַע דַּעְתּוֹ הִתִּירוֹ וְשָׂם הַדָּבָר בְּפִיו, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שבת קד ע״א) ״בָּא לְטַמֵּא פּוֹתְחִין לוֹ״; וְעוֹד שֶׁיֵּדְעוּ בְּנֵי אָדָם כִּי בְּדִין נֶעֱנַשׁ.
Radak הָיָ֣ה עָר֔וּם
Hebrew
חָכָם, וַאֲשֶׁר הוּא עִנְיַן חָכְמָה הוּא בְּשׁוּרֻק, וַאֲשֶׁר הוּא עִנְיַן עָרוֹם הוּא בְּחוֹלָם; וְכֵן הָרִבּוּי אֲשֶׁר הוּא לְשׁוֹן חָכְמָה הַמֵּ״ם רָפָה כְּמוֹ ״מַחְשְׁבוֹת עֲרוּמִים״ (איוב ה:יב) וַאֲשֶׁר הוּא לְשׁוֹן עָרוֹם הַמֵּ״ם בְּדָגֵשׁ, כְּמוֹ ״וּבִגְדֵי עֲרוּמִּים תַּפְשִׁיט״ (איוב כב:ו). וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר
Radak הָיָ֣ה עָר֔וּם
Hebrew
רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר חָכָם וְעָרוּם בְּכֹחַ הַדִּמְיוֹן אֲשֶׁר לַבְּהֵמָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל הַשּׁוּעָל שֶׁהוּא עָרוּם וּבַעַל תַּחְבּוּלוֹת וְזֶהוּ בְּכֹחַ הַדִּמְיוֹן וְלֹא בְּכֹחַ הַשֵּׂכֶל כִּי אֵין כֹּחַ הַשֵּׂכֶל בַּשְּׁפָלִים, אֶלָּא לָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ, וְהַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם וּבַעַל תַּחְבּוּלוֹת יוֹתֵר מֵהַשּׁוּעָל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר
Radak מִכֹּל֙ חַיַּ֣ת הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה
Hebrew
, וְלֹא זָכַר הַבְּהֵמָה לְפִי שֶׁחַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה יֵשׁ בָּהֶן יוֹתֵר עַרְמִימִיּוּת מִן הַבְּהֵמוֹת הַגְּדוֹלוֹת וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן הַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם יוֹתֵר מֵהֶן וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר מֵהַבְּהֵמוֹת. וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר
Radak אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֖ה יְהֹוָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֑ים
Hebrew
, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכֻּלָּם עָשָׂה אוֹתָם בְּחֹמֶר אֶחָד, שָׂם בָּהֶם לְאַחַת יִתְרוֹן עַל חֲבֶרְתָּהּ, יֵשׁ בְּעָרְמָה וְיֵשׁ בִּגְבוּרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁרָאָה הָאֵל בְּחָכְמָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר לֹא תֻּשַּׂג.
Radak וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ אֶל הָ֣אִשָּׁ֔ה
Hebrew
וְלֹא אָמַר לְאָדָם, הָאִשָּׁה קְרוֹבָה לְהִתְפַּתּוֹת יוֹתֵר מִן הָאִישׁ, כִּי דַּעְתָּהּ קַלָּה.
Radakrecords אַ֚ף כִּֽי אָמַ֣ר אֱלֹהִ֔ים
Radak: 'אף' means 'in addition': other words passed between the woman and the serpent, and Scripture gives only the end of the talk, as with 'כי' in Joshua 2:24.
Hebrew
בְּאָמְרוֹ אַף שֶׁמּוֹרֶה תּוֹסֶפֶת עַל הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁקָּדְמוּ, נִרְאֶה כִּי דְּבָרִים אֲחֵרִים קָדְמוּ בֵּין חַוָּה וּבֵין הַנָּחָשׁ, וְדוֹמֶה שֶׁאָמְרָה חַוָּה לַנָּחָשׁ עַל הַכָּבוֹד שֶׁעָשָׂה לָהֶם הָאֵל שֶׁהִשְׁכִּינָם בְּגַן עֵדֶן, אָמַר לָהּ הַנָּחָשׁ אֲנִי רוֹאֶה שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שׂוֹנֵא אֶתְכֶם אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִגְדִּיל אֶתְכֶם מִשְּׁאָר הַיְצוּרִים שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲשֶׂה לָכֶם מַעֲלָה כָּךְ וְכָךְ, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁאָמַר אֲלֵיכֶם שֶׁלֹּא תֹאכְלוּ מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן בָּזֶה תּוּכְלוּ לְהַכִּיר שֶׁהוּא שׂוֹנֵא אֶתְכֶם וְאֵינְכֶם חֲשׁוּבִים בְּעֵינָיו כְּמוֹ שֶׁאַתְּ אוֹמֶרֶת, וְהַכָּתוּב הִנִּיחַ רָאשֵׁי הַדְּבָרִים וְלָקַח סוֹפָם, וְכֵן הוּא מִנְהַג הַכָּתוּב בִּמְקוֹמוֹת רַבּוֹת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ הַמְרַגְּלִים אֶל יְהוֹשֻׁעַ (יהושע ב:כד) ״כִּי נָתַן ה׳ בְּיָדֵנוּ אֶת כָּל הָאָרֶץ״ וְאֵין מִלַּת ״כִּי״ תְּחִלַּת הַדְּבָרִים. וּפֵרֵשׁ

Apparatus
  • Onkelos: חַכִּים 'wise' for עָרוּם, and בְּקוּשְׁטָא 'in truth' for אַף כִּי.
  • Sforno: the serpent is the evil inclination, which Scripture names after the creature it resembles; Ibn Ezra rejects the view that it was Satan. Radak records the midrash of the serpent ridden by Samael.
  • Radak (3:1:4) and Ibn Ezra differ on the nature of the serpent's wisdom: Radak says it was cunning of the imaginative faculty found in animals, as in the fox, not the intellect; Ibn Ezra says it was a real, if limited, wisdom.
  • Ibn Ezra and Radak read אַף כִּי as 'how much more, that God said ...', the end of a longer exchange, not a question; Rashi reads a question, 'perhaps He said ...'. The English follows Rashi.
3:2

The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat from the fruit of the trees of the garden.”

and-said the-woman to the-serpent from-fruit-of tree-of the-garden we-eat

Grammar
  • מִפְּרִי עֵץ־הַגָּן stands before the verb for contrast: of these we eat (the next verse gives the one tree not eaten from).
  • עֵץ־ is singular in form and collective in sense, 'the trees of the garden', as in 3:1; the maqqef joins it to הַגָּן in a construct chain.
  • נֹאכֵל has tsere for the usual patah: a pausal form, because it carries the silluq at the end of the verse.
  • The yiqtol states what is allowed or habitual: 'we eat' and 'we may eat' are both possible; the English chooses 'may' because she answers a question about what is forbidden.

Her answer is brief and corrects the serpent's overstatement by naming what is permitted (Radak): not every tree was forbidden, only one.

Commentary (3)
Radakfollows וַתֹּ֥אמֶר
Radak: it is not as you say; He did not forbid every tree of the garden, only one, in the middle of the garden. He forbade it for our good, perhaps because its fruit is deadly by nature.

Apparatus
  • Sforno: the woman is dragged into the risk by imagination and her weak mind, and imputes jealousy to God; a reading of her motive, not of the words.
3:3

As for the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God said, “You must not eat from it, and you must not touch it, or you might die.”

and-from-fruit-of the-tree which in-midst-of the-garden said God not you-eat from-it and-not you-touch in-it lest you-die

Grammar
  • וּמִפְּרִי הָעֵץ אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹךְ־הַגָּן is a fronted phrase with a relative clause, set against מִפְּרִי עֵץ־הַגָּן of the previous verse: all these, but of this one.
  • The revia on אֱלֹהִים divides the introduction from the speech; the zinor and segol on הָעֵץ and הַגָּן mark the relative clause as a unit.
  • לֹא תֹאכְלוּ and וְלֹא תִגְּעוּ are two prohibitions in the yiqtol; the second is not in the commandment of 2:17.
  • פֶּן with the yiqtol states what is feared; תְּמֻתוּן has the paragogic nun and the full pausal ending.
  • The pack parses מִמֶּנּוּ as 1st plural; the same form is 3rd masculine singular, and the context gives 'from it'.

The woman does not name the tree and she speaks of God's word without the name יְהוָה. She quotes the prohibition with 'touch', which is not in 2:16–17; Rashi counts this as an addition to the command. פֶּן is rendered 'or you might die' to keep the ambiguity: 'lest' (a fear of what follows), or 'perhaps' (Radak records the second as an alternative).

Commentary (5)
Rashinormativefollows וְלֹ֥א תִגְּע֖וּ בּ֑וֹ
Rashi: she added to the command, and so came to loss, as it says, 'Do not add to His words' (Prov. 30:6). The English gives her words as spoken, with 'touch' as hers.

Radakrecords פֶּן
Radak: פֶּן means 'perhaps'; God had said she would surely die, but for the added 'touch' she says 'lest', because she herself added it; or the sense is 'that you not die', as in 'lest you take my son back there' (24:6). The English 'might' leaves both open.
