מִתְמַעֶטֶת וְהוֹלֶכֶת דּוֹר אַחַר דּוֹר:
Radaknot-applicable וַיִּֽהְי֣וּ יְמֵי אָדָ֗ם
Radak: those named were the ones born in the image and likeness; the other sons and daughters were not, and were blotted out in the flood. He also records Maimonides' view on the long ages.

Grammar

Grammar
  • אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ is a preposition with an infinitive construct and subject suffix: 'after his begetting'.

and-were all-of days-of Kenan ten years and-nine hundred year and-died

Grammar
  • כָּל־יְמֵי קֵינָן is a construct chain: 'all the days of Kenan'.
  • עֶשֶׂר שָׁנִים: ten, with plural 'years'; the larger number follows with singular שָׁנָה.
  • וַיִּהְיוּ is plural because its subject is the plural יְמֵי, 'days', not כָּל.
  • וַיָּמֹת is the wayyiqtol of מות in pause (silluq). The usual form is וַיָּמָת, the short form with the stress drawn back; in pause the stress stays on the last syllable and the ḥolem returns.
  • The paragraph mark ס closes the entry for Kenan.

  • The mahpakh on חָמֵשׁ is a conjunctive accent: it joins חָמֵשׁ to וְתִשְׁעִים. The pashta on וְתִשְׁעִים is the disjunctive that sets the number off from שָׁנָה, which has the zaqef qaton.
  • The paragraph mark ס closes the entry for Mahalalel.

The total 895 is 65 plus 830.

Grammar
  • The numeral is built units first: שְׁתַּיִם וְשִׁשִּׁים שָׁנָה וּמְאַת שָׁנָה, 'two and sixty years and a hundred years'.
  • וַיּוֹלֶד is Hifil wayyiqtol of ילד; the Hifil is the regular verb for a father's begetting.
  • The etnaḥta on שָׁנָה (second) divides the verse between the age and the birth.

Standard formulaic verse of the Adam genealogy; the age is the age at the birth of the named son.

The English keeps the Hebrew order of clauses by setting the time clause between commas.

Targum Onkelos the whole verse

Grammar
  • וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ is Hitpael: 'walked about, walked habitually', here of a way of life.
  • אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים: אֶת here is the preposition 'with', so 'walked with God', not an object marker.
  • The formula 'and he lived' is replaced by 'and he walked with God': the change marks Enoch.
  • The three hundred years run from the birth of Methuselah, not from Enoch's birth.

Ibn Ezra reads the walking as following God, like 'you shall walk after the LORD your God' (Deut 13:5); 'with God' keeps the preposition's plain sense. Radak, who is not normative, dates the beginning of Enoch's devotion to the sixty-fifth year.

Commentary (1)
Targum Onkelosnot-applicable the whole verse
Onkelos reproduces the figures (תְּלַת מְאָה וְשִׁתִּין וַחֲמֵשׁ).
Hebrew
וַהֲוָה כָּל יוֹמֵי חֲנוֹךְ תְּלַת מְאָה וְשִׁתִּין וַחֲמֵשׁ שְׁנִין:
5:24 · ס

Enoch walked with God, and he was no more, for God took him.

and-walked Enoch with the-God and-not-he for took [object-marker]-him God

Grammar
  • וְאֵינֶנּוּ is the particle אֵין with a suffix: 'and he was not'. It is a verbless clause.
  • לָקַח אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים: verb, pronoun object, then noun subject. A pronoun object regularly comes before a noun subject, so the order is the ordinary one and gives no special stress.
  • The etnaḥta on הָאֱלֹהִים closes the first half; the zaqef gadol on וְאֵינֶנּוּ separates the disappearance from its reason.
  • The first אֱלֹהִים has the article (the true God); the second does not, and is the subject.

Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that וְאֵינֶנּוּ ... לָקַח means that Enoch died, and the English 'he was no more, for God took him' carries that reading. They differ on its character: for Rashi a death before his time, for Ibn Ezra a death without plague or 'and he died', a taking 'with glory' (Ps 73:24). Radak records the view of the Targum and some sages that Enoch entered Eden alive; it is not the plain sense.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows וַיִּתְהַלֵּ֥ךְ חֲנ֖וֹךְ
Rashi (from Genesis Rabbah): Enoch was righteous but easily moved to turn to wickedness (קַל בְּדַעְתּוֹ לָשׁוּב לְהַרְשִׁיעַ), so God hastened to remove him and made him die before his time. That is why the text writes his death differently, וְאֵינֶנּוּ: he was not in the world to fill out his years (וְאֵינֶנּוּ בָּעוֹלָם לְמַלְּאוֹת שְׁנוֹתָיו).

, כְּלוֹמַר לָקַח נַפְשׁוֹ וְהֶעֱלָה אוֹתָהּ אֶל הָעֶלְיוֹנִים, וְכֵן ״אַחַר כָּבוֹד תִּקָּחֵנִי״ (תהלים עג:כד), ״כִּי יִקָּחֵנִי סֶלָה״ (תהלים מט:טז), וְנֶפֶשׁ הָרָשָׁע לֹא יִקַּח אוֹתָהּ אֱלֹהִים אֶלָּא תֵּרֵד שְׁאוֹל. וְאֵין כֵּן (יחזקאל כד:טז) ״הִנְנִי לֹקֵחַ אֶת־מַחְמַד עֵינֶיךָ בְּמַגֵּפָה״, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמַר הִנְנִי לֹקֵחַ שֶׁיִּדָּמֶה שֶׁהָיְתָה טוֹבָה וַחֲסוּדָה, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁהָיְתָה אֵשֶׁת נָבִיא, אַף עַל פִּי כֵן לֹא הָיְתָה שְׁלֵמָה, לְפִיכָךְ אָמַר בְּמַגֵּפָה, כִּי כְּאֵב אָנוּשׁ הָיָה לָהּ בְּעֵת הַמִּיתָה וְזֶהוּ מַגֵּפָה. וְכֵן ״כִּי־יִגֹּף שׁוֹר אִישׁ אֶת־שׁוֹר רֵעֵהוּ וָמֵת״ (שמות כא:לה), הִנֵּה כִּי הַמַּגֵּפָה הִיא מַכָּה אֲנוּשָׁה, אֲבָל הִיא מַכַּת פִּתְאֹם בְּלִי קְדִימַת חֹלִי. אֲבָל ״וְרַגְלְךָ לֹא תִגּוֹף״ (משלי ג:כג) הִיא מַכָּה בְּלֹא מִיתָה אֲבָל הִיא מַכָּה אֲנוּשָׁה; אֲבָל הַשְּׁלֵמִים אֵין לָהֶם מַגֵּפָה בְּעֵת מִיתָתָם. וְדַעַת הַתַּרְגּוּם גַּם קְצָת חֲכָמִים (מסכת דרך ארץ) כִּי חֲנוֹךְ וְאֵלִיָּהוּ הִכְנִיסָם הָאֵל חַיִּים בְּגַן עֵדֶן בְּנֶפֶשׁ וּבְבָשָׂר וְעוֹדָם שָׁם חַיִּים אוֹכְלִים מִפְּרִי הָעֵץ וְעוֹבְדִים אֶת ה׳ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קֹדֶם שֶׁחָטָא, וְיִהְיוּ שָׁם עַד יְמוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ. יֵשׁ לִשְׁאֹל: כִּי בְּסִפּוּר אֵלֶּה הַתּוֹלְדוֹת מֵאָדָם וְעַד נֹחַ אָמַר וַיָּמֹת, וּבְסִפּוּר תּוֹלְדוֹת נֹחַ לֹא אָמַר כֵּן? וְאָמְרוּ: לְפִי שֶׁמֵּתוּ בַּמַּבּוּל אָמַר בְּאֵלֶּה וַיָּמֹת. וּלְדַעְתֵּנוּ, כִּי הַנִּזְכָּרִים הָיוּ צַדִּיקִים וְטוֹבִים, לֹא מֵת אֶחָד מֵהֶם בַּמַּבּוּל, אֶלָּא תּוֹלְדוֹתֵיהֶם שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ טוֹבִים, וְכָל אֵלֶּה מֵתוּ קֹדֶם הַמַּבּוּל כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּמְצָא בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן יְמֵיהֶם. וְהַנָּכוֹן, לְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ שְׁנוֹתֵיהֶם אֲרֻכִּים מְאֹד אָמַר בָּהֶם וַיָּמֹת, כְּלוֹמַר חָיוּ כָּל אֵלֶּה הַשָּׁנִים וְהוֹלִידוּ תּוֹלְדוֹת וְאַחַר מֵתוּ, אֲבָל בְּסִפּוּר הַתּוֹלְדוֹת מִנֹּחַ וְעַד אַבְרָהָם לֹא הָיוּ כָּל כָּךְ מֻפְלָגִים בְּחַיֵּיהֶם, לֹא אָמַר בָּהֶם וַיָּמֹת.

Apparatus
  • Enoch's departure is described by the verb לָקַח, 'take'; the verse does not say 'and he died'.
5:25

Methuselah lived one hundred eighty-seven years, and he fathered Lamech.

and-lived Methuselah seven and-eighty year and-hundred-of year and-he-fathered [object-marker] Lamech

Grammar
  • The age is given units first: 'seven and eighty year and hundred year'; English reverses it to 'one hundred eighty-seven'.
  • וַיְחִי and וַיּוֹלֶד are wayyiqtols: the narrative chain of the genealogy.
  • The tevir on וּשְׁמֹנִים and tipḥa on שָׁנָה mark off the units and tens; the etnaḥta on the second שָׁנָה ends the first half of the verse.

Fixed genealogical formula; the 'year' is repeated after the tens and after the hundreds.

Commentary (1)
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Onkelos renders the verse closely: Methuselah lived one hundred eighty-seven years and begot Lamech; he reverses the order of the numbers as the English does.
Hebrew
וַחֲיָא מְתוּשֶׁלַח מְאָה וְתַמְנִין וּשְׁבַע שְׁנִין וְאוֹלִיד יָת לָמֶךְ:
5:26

Methuselah lived, after he fathered Lamech, seven hundred eighty-two years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

and-lived Methuselah after fathering-him [object-marker] Lamech two and-eighty year and-seven hundreds year and-he-fathered sons and-daughters

Grammar
  • אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ is a preposition plus infinitive construct with suffix: 'after his begetting', rendered as a clause.
  • The accents (pashta on אַחֲרֵי, zaqef on לֶמֶךְ) set the 'after' clause apart before the number of years.
  • שְׁתַּיִם is the feminine form of 'two' before the feminine שָׁנָה.
  • בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת is a merism: all further children, unnamed.

Here the number is 'two and eighty' then 'seven hundreds'.

Grammar
  • כָּל־יְמֵי מְתוּשֶׁלַח is a construct chain: 'all the days of Methuselah'.
  • The verb וַיִּהְיוּ is plural although the sum of years is one figure: it agrees with 'days'.
  • וַיָּמֹת closes the entry with the formula of death; the silluq ends the verse and the ס marks a paragraph break.

The total is the sum of 187 + 782 = 969 years.

Grammar
  • The pattern repeats from verse 25, with 'two' in place of 'seven'.

Rashi's midrashic remark on 'a son' is a homily, not a reading of the words.

Commentary (2)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וַיּ֖וֹלֶד בֵּֽן׃
Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah: שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ נִבְנָה הָעוֹלָם, 'from him the world was built', a play on בֵּן and בנה. It is a homily and does not alter the plain sense.

שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ נִבְנָה הָעוֹלָם (בראשית רבה):
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Onkelos: Lamech lived one hundred eighty-two years and begot a son, as in the English.
Hebrew
וַחֲיָא לֶמֶךְ מְאָה וְתַמְנִין וְתַרְתֵּין שְׁנִין וְאוֹלִיד בָּר:
5:29

He named him Noah, saying, "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the toil of our hands, from the ground that the LORD has cursed."

and-he-called [object-marker] name-his Noah saying this he-will-comfort-us from-work-our and-from-toil-of hands-our from-the-ground which cursed-it the-LORD

Grammar
  • The name נֹחַ is explained by wordplay with יְנַחֲמֵנוּ: the sounds נ-ח (root נוח 'rest', root נחם 'comfort') are close but not identical.
  • יְנַחֲמֵנוּ is Piel imperfect with the 1st plural suffix: 'he will comfort us'.
  • The gershayim and telisha gedola on זֶה mark a rare accent and give it weight at the opening of the quotation.
  • אֵרְרָהּ is a Piel perfect with a feminine suffix referring to הָאֲדָמָה; the antecedent is the ground, cursed in 3:17.
  • 'The LORD' stands last in the verse, after the verb, with the silluq.

The saying explains the name; the pun is only approximate. The English 'bring us relief' follows Rashi (יָנַח מִמֶּנּוּ, 'he will ease from us') and Ibn Ezra ('this one will comfort us, and we will rest from the toil of our hands'; נֶחָמָה is rest from grief), who both read the word through נוח; the usual Piel sense 'comfort' (BDB) is kept in the literal line and the grammar notes. The meaning of the name is kept out of the English line.

Commentary (10)
Rashinormativefollows זֶ֞֠ה יְנַחֲמֵ֤נוּ
Rashi: זֶה יְנַחֲמֵנוּ means יָנַח מִמֶּנּוּ אֶת עִצְּבוֹן יָדֵינוּ, 'he will ease from us the toil of our hands'. Before Noah they had no ploughing tools and he made them; the ground, under the first Adam's curse, put out thorns and thistles when wheat was sown, and in Noah's days it rested. Read otherwise, the sense does not fit the name, and he would have had to be called מְנַחֵם.
Hebrew
יָנַח מִמֶּנּוּ אֶת עִצְּבוֹן יָדֵינוּ. עַד שֶׁלֹּא בָא נֹחַ לֹא הָיָה לָהֶם כְּלֵי מַחֲרֵשָׁה וְהוּא הֵכִין לָהֶם וְהָיְתָה הָאָרֶץ מוֹצִיאָה קוֹצִים וְדַרְדַּרִים כְּשֶׁזּוֹרְעִים חִטִּים, מִקִּלְלָתוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, וּבִימֵי נֹחַ נָחָה, וְזֶהוּ יְנַחֲמֵנוּ, וְאִם לֹא תְפָרְשֵׁהוּ כָּךְ אֵין טַעַם הַלָּשׁוֹן נוֹפֵל עַל הַשֵּׁם וְאַתָּה צָרִיךְ לִקְרוֹת שְׁמוֹ מְנַחֵם:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: Lamech knew through Adam, being a prophet, or saw by wisdom, that through this child the ground would revive; and so it was, for through him the world endured, and he was a man of the ground. Or he was named Noah afterwards, as Jerubbaal was, once he had worked the ground and it prospered. The sense is 'this one will comfort us, and we will rest (וְנָנוּחַ) from the toil of our hands'; comfort is rest from grief of heart (עִצְּבוֹן הַלֵּב), for Hebrew keeps the sense and not the exact word, as יְרֻבַּעַל and יְרֻבֶּשֶׁת show.

5:30

Lamech lived, after he fathered Noah, five hundred ninety-five years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

and-lived-Lamech after fathering-him [object-marker] Noah five and-ninety year and-five hundreds year and-he-fathered sons and-daughters

Grammar
  • The structure is the same as verse 26, with Noah in place of Lamech.
  • חָמֵשׁ is the feminine form of 'five' with שָׁנָה; מֵאֹת is the plural of מֵאָה spelled defectively, without the vav (elsewhere מֵאוֹת); the vowel is the same ḥolem.
  • The munaḥ on הוֹלִידוֹ joins it to אֶת־נֹחַ, and the zaqef qaton on נֹחַ closes the temporal clause before the number of years.
  • The revia on לֶמֶךְ marks the subject before the temporal clause.

Grammar
  • The verse repeats the formula of 5:27 for Lamech.
  • The singular verb וַיְהִי (here) agrees with the sum as a whole, unlike the plural וַיִּהְיוּ in 5:27.
  • The total is 595 + 182 = 777 years.
  • The ס after the verse marks a paragraph break.

and-was Noah son-of five hundreds year and-fathered Noah [object-marker] Shem [object-marker] Ham and-[object-marker] Japheth

Grammar
  • בֶּן־חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה is the age formula: 'son of five hundred years'.
  • The etnaḥta on שָׁנָה divides the verse: Noah's age, then the births.
  • וַיּוֹלֶד is Hifil wayyiqtol of ילד, 'he fathered'.
  • The three sons are each marked by אֶת; the list is joined by ו only before the last.

The order Shem, Ham, Japheth is the order of the text; Rashi and Radak (following Bereshit Rabbah) discuss which son was eldest, which does not change the English.

Commentary (5)
Rashinormativenot-applicable בֶּן חֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת שָׁנָ֑ה
Rashi (from Bereshit Rabbah): every earlier generation begot at about a hundred, but Noah at five hundred. God said: if his sons are wicked they will perish in the water, and that is hard for this righteous man; if they are righteous I would burden him with building many arks. So God restrained his fountain (כָּבַשׁ אֶת מַעְיָנוֹ) until five hundred, so that Japheth, the eldest, would not reach a hundred, the age of liability to punishment, before the Flood. A homily on the age, not on the words' sense.

6:1

When humankind began to multiply over the surface of the ground and daughters were born to them,

and-it-was when began the-human to-multiply upon face-of the-ground and-daughters were-born to-them

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי כִּי introduces a temporal clause: 'and it was when'.
  • הֵחֵל is Hifil perfect of חלל, 'begin' (a different verb from חלל 'profane').
  • לָרֹב is an infinitive construct, 'to multiply'.
  • יֻלְּדוּ is Pual: 'were born', with an indefinite plural subject.

הָאָדָם with the article is normally 'the human' (decisions); here the sense is collective (Radak: מִין הָאָדָם, the species), so 'humankind' is used. The 'daughters' are those of the human race generally.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos: כַּד שְׁרִיאוּ בְנֵי אֱנָשָׁא לְמִסְגֵּי, 'when the children of men began to increase'.
6:2

The sons of the rulers saw that the daughters of humankind were beautiful, and they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.

and-saw sons-of the-gods [object-marker] daughters-of the-human that good they and-took for-them women from-all that they-chose

Grammar
  • בְנֵי־הָאֱלֹהִים is a construct chain with a plural noun in the absolute and the article; the sense of אֱלֹהִים is the main difficulty.
  • כִּי טֹבֹת הֵנָּה is a verbless clause: 'that they were good'. The feminine pronoun הֵנָּה refers to the daughters.
  • וַיִּקְחוּ לָהֶם נָשִׁים: 'took for themselves women', the idiom for marrying.
  • מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּחָרוּ is 'from all whom they chose' (all that they chose); Rashi and Radak read it as including women already married.

Per decisions, אֱלֹהִים of beings other than the God of Israel takes the sense of the normative commentators. Here they differ. Rashi's first reading, with Onkelos (בני רברביא), Ramban and Radak, is 'the sons of the princes and judges' (Rashi: every אֱלֹהִים in Scripture is an expression of authority), and Ibn Ezra lists it first; the English follows Rashi. Rashi's other reading (the angelic princes who go on God's errands) and Ibn Ezra's others (the holy ones; the sons of Seth; and his own preference, those who knew the knowledge of the Most High and chose their wives by the order of the heavens) are recorded below. The Hebrew טֹבֹת is spelled defectively; Rashi's homily from the spelling is not an issue for the plain sense.

Commentary (14)
Rashinormativefollows בְנֵי הָֽאֱלֹהִים֙
Rashi: בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים are the sons of the princes and judges; every אֱלֹהִים in Scripture is an expression of authority (cf. Ex 4:16, 7:1). His second reading, the officers who go on God's mission mingling with them, is recorded.

Ibn Ezranormativerecords בְנֵי הָֽאֱלֹהִים֙
Ibn Ezra lists readings of בני האלהים: the sons of the judges, who did God's justice on earth; some say that אלהים here means 'holy' and the sons are the holy ones, as in 'you are children' (Dt 14:1); some say the sons of Seth, the daughters being of Cain's family. 'The right in my eyes' (והישר בעיני) is that they were those who knew the knowledge of the Most High and chose wives whose configuration of the heavens matched each man, so that their offspring were like the begetting, and mighty men came from them; they may also have taken the women by force. The English follows Rashi's 'rulers', the first reading Ibn Ezra lists, not his preference.

Apparatus
  • אֱלֹהִים here: rulers or judges (Rashi's first reading, the first Ibn Ezra lists, Ramban, Radak, Onkelos בני רברביא); the angelic princes who go on God's errands (Rashi's other reading; Radak calls the midrash of Azza and Azael far-fetched); 'the holy ones' (reported by Ibn Ezra); the sons of Seth, with the daughters of Cain's line (reported by Ibn Ezra); those who knew the knowledge of the Most High and chose their wives by the order of the heavens (Ibn Ezra's own preference, quoted by Radak).
  • Onkelos renders טֹבֹת with שַׁפִּירָן, 'beautiful'.
  • בָּחָרוּ: Onkelos has דִּי אִתְרְעִיאוּ, 'whom they desired'.
6:3

Then the LORD said, "My spirit will not contend over humankind for long, since they are also flesh; their days will be one hundred and twenty years."

and-said the-LORD not will-contend my-spirit in-the-human for-ever in-since-also he flesh and-will-be his-days hundred and-twenty year

Grammar
  • יָדוֹן is a rare and disputed form. Rashi: it means 'quarrel, contend' (he speaks of a מָדוֹן, a strife, in God's spirit). Ibn Ezra reports two views: 'sheath' (as נָדָן, 1 Chr 21:27, the body being the spirit's sheath), with ידון then from another, hollow root; or from דין, 'judge'. His own sense is 'will not abide' (לֹא יַעֲמֹד). Radak explains the 'sheath' form as a lost nun.
  • בְּשַׁגַּם: Rashi and Ibn Ezra take the שַׁ as the relative שֶׁ, with the vowel changed: 'since also'.
  • וְהָיוּ is a weqatal: the days 'will be' 120 years, a grant of time.
  • The etnaḥta after בָשָׂר divides the verse into the sentence of decision and the term granted.

The English follows Rashi on ידון (contend, quarrel) and לעלם (for a long time), and Rashi and Ibn Ezra on בשגם (since also). The 120 years is read as a respite (Rashi, Sforno, Onkelos), not as the future length of a human life, which Ibn Ezra rejects as untrue. 'My spirit' is God's. The reading 'sheath' and the reading 'judge' are recorded. The lexicon lists a sense under דין for this form; the Qal 6 'contend' is the closest in the list.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos: לָא יִתְקַיַם דָרָא בִישָׁא הָדֵין קֳדָמַי לְעַלָם ... אַרְכָא יְהִיבַת לְהוֹן מְאָה וְעַשְׂרִין שְׁנִין אִם יְתוּבוּן, 'this evil generation will not stand before me for ever ... a respite of 120 years is given them if they repent'.
  • יָדוֹן: 'contend' (Rashi), 'abide', as in a sheath (Ibn Ezra's first), or 'judge' (Ibn Ezra's second); the written form is not otherwise attested.
  • The pointing of the divine name is יְהֹוָה (MAM) and is read as 'the LORD'.
6:4 · פ

The giants were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, whenever the sons of the rulers came to the daughters of humankind and they bore children to them. They were the warriors of old, the men of renown.

the-Nephilim were in-the-earth in-the-days the-those and-also after-so that will-come sons-of the-gods to daughters-of the-human and-bore to-them they the-warriors that from-ever men-of the-name

Grammar
  • הַנְּפִלִים: Rashi says that in Hebrew the word means 'giants' (עֲנָקִים), and gives a reason for the name: they fell and made the world fall. Ibn Ezra and Radak: the heart of one who sees them falls, astonished at their height.
  • יָבֹאוּ is a yiqtol after אֲשֶׁר that, with the weqatal וְיָלְדוּ, expresses repeated action: 'whenever they came ... and bore'.
  • הֵמָּה הַגִּבֹּרִים is a verbless clause: the pronoun הֵמָּה ('they') is the subject and הַגִּבֹּרִים the predicate. The darga on הֵמָּה is conjunctive and binds it to the next word; the tevir on הַגִּבֹּרִים is disjunctive.
  • מֵעוֹלָם: 'from of old', from long ago; אַנְשֵׁי הַשֵּׁם: 'men of the name', men of fame.

הַנְּפִלִים is rendered 'giants': Rashi says this is the word's meaning in Hebrew (לְשׁוֹן עֲנָקִים), Ibn Ezra and Radak explain the name by their height, and the lexicon gives 'giants'; the transliteration 'Nephilim' is given in the token note. וְגַם אַחֲרֵי כֵן: Rashi 'afterward', even though they had seen the destruction of the generation of Enosh; Ibn Ezra 'after the Flood'. The English 'and also afterward' keeps both. הַגִּבֹּרִים are 'warriors' (mighty men); Rashi adds 'to rebel against God'. אַנְשֵׁי הַשֵּׁם: Rashi gives two midrashic readings: the men designated by names that speak of destruction (Irad, Mehujael, Methushael), and 'men of desolation' (שִׁמָּמוֹן). The English 'men of renown' follows Radak (they had a name in the mouths of later generations) and Onkelos (אֱנָשִׁין דִּשְׁמָא); Rashi's readings are recorded. The lexicon lists a single sense for the Nephilim entry, which is not a path; the sense is therefore omitted below.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos: גִּבָּרַיָּא הֲווֹ בְאַרְעָא בְּיוֹמַיָּא הָאִנּוּן, 'the mighty ones were in the land in those days', rendering נפלים as גבריא; and 'sons of the nobles' for בני האלהים.
  • אַחֲרֵי כֵן: after the destruction of Enosh's generation (Rashi) or after the Flood (Ibn Ezra, Ramban's report); kept open.
  • The paragraph mark פ follows this verse.
6:5

The LORD saw that the evil of the human was great on the earth, and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all day long.

and-saw the-LORD that great evil-of the-human in-the-earth and-every formation-of thoughts-of his-heart only evil all-the-day

Grammar
  • וַיַּרְא is a wayyiqtol; כִּי introduces the object clause: what the LORD saw.
  • רַבָּה רָעַת הָאָדָם: the predicate adjective comes first, and the verb 'to be' is not written. רָעַת is the construct of רָעָה.
  • וְכׇל־יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ is a chain of constructs (every / inclination / of thoughts / of his heart) with no verb; רַק רַע is its predicate.
  • The etnaḥta on בָּאָרֶץ divides the verse: the evil on the earth, and then the inward cause.

יֵצֶר is from יצר 'to form, shape'; Radak takes it as the desire of the heart's thinking, which forms and works out matters within the heart. The English 'inclination' follows that. הָאָדָם is 'the human', mankind generally (a collective), per decisions.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos renders the verse closely: 'and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all day' (יִצְרָא מַחְשְׁבַת לִבֵּהּ לְחוֹד בִּישׁ כָּל יוֹמָא).
6:6

The LORD regretted that he had made the human on the earth, and was grieved in his heart.

and-regretted the-LORD that-made [object-mark] the-human in-the-earth and-grieved-himself to his-heart

Grammar
  • וַיִּנָּחֶם is a Niphal wayyiqtol; the stem is reflexive-passive, 'he let himself be sorry'.
  • וַיִּתְעַצֵּב is a Hithpael wayyiqtol, 'he pained himself'; it is the counterpart of the Niphal verb before it.
  • אֶל־לִבּוֹ: the phrase is literally 'to his heart', the inward place of thought and feeling.
  • The etnaḥta on בָּאָרֶץ divides the verse: the regret over the making, and then the grief.

The two verbs speak of God in human terms. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Ramban all say the Torah speaks in human language, so the English keeps the verbs plain ('regretted', 'was grieved'). Rashi reads otherwise: first, וַיִּנָּחֶם as consolation (it comforted God that man was made among the lower beings); then, as a change of thought from mercy to judgment, 'he considered what to do'. Both Rashi readings are recorded. בָּאָרֶץ (on the earth) modifies the making: Radak reads it as made of earth.

Commentary (17)
Rashinormativerecords וַיִּנָּ֣חֶם יְהֹוָ֔ה כִּֽי עָשָׂ֥ה
Rashi: נֶחָמָה here is consolation: it was a comfort before God that he had created man among the lower beings, for had he been one of the upper beings he would have led them to rebel. On this reading וַיִּנָּחֶם means 'was consoled', not 'regretted'; the English follows Ibn Ezra's 'regretted' (in human language) and keeps this reading here.

6:7

The LORD said, "I will wipe out the human whom I created from the face of the ground, from human to beast, to creeping thing, and to the birds of the sky, for I regret that I made them."

and-said the-LORD I-will-wipe-out [object-mark] the-human whom I-created from-upon faces-of the-ground from-human until beast until creeping-thing and-until bird-of the-heavens that I-regret that I-made-them

Grammar
  • אֶמְחֶה is a first-person imperfect of מחה, 'wipe', and states a resolve; Rashi reads the verb as fitting dust, which water wipes out.
  • The list מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה עַד־רֶמֶשׂ וְעַד־עוֹף הַשָּׁמָיִם uses עַד for the limits of what is destroyed; the last item takes וְ.
  • The two clauses with כִּי form a pair: כִּי נִחַמְתִּי (Niphal) and כִּי עֲשִׂיתִם (Qal), so the regret is tied to the making.
  • The etnaḥta on הַשָּׁמָיִם divides the verse: the decree, and then the reason.

The speech is addressed to no one stated. Ibn Ezra's own view is that it is joined to 'his heart' of verse 6 (the speech is inward), and Radak allows 'to Noah'; the English gives the bare 'said'. אֶת־הָאָדָם is 'the human' (mankind), per decisions. 'Whom I created' uses בָּרָא, the verb of Genesis 1, which the lexicon lists as Qal.

6:8 · פ

But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.

and-Noah found favor in-eyes-of the-LORD

Grammar
  • וְנֹחַ מָצָא: the subject comes before the verb, so the clause is a contrast with the preceding judgment; hence 'But'.
  • מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי is an idiom for 'was acceptable to', literally 'found favor in the eyes of'.
  • The zaqef gadol on נֹחַ marks Noah as the subject standing apart, and the silluq closes the paragraph (פ).

The vav is rendered 'But', following the contrast. The lexicon's עַיִן senses list 5 for 'in the presence of', which is the idiom's sense; the sense 2.b etc. are for other uses.

לְהַצִּיל גַּם בָּנָיו וּבְנוֹתָיו לֹא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה רָאוּי לְכָךְ, אֲבָל עַל צַד חֲנִינָה זִכָּהוּ הָאֵל יִתְבָּרַךְ לָזֶה, כְּאָמְרוֹ: "וּשְׁלֹשֶׁת הָאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה בְּתוֹכָהּ נֹחַ דָּנִיֵּאל וְאִיּוֹב חַי ה' אִם בָּנִים וְאִם בָּנוֹת יַצִּילוּ הֵמָּה לְבַדָּם יִנָּצֵלוּ" (יחזקאל יד:יד). וְזֶה כִּי לֹא לִמְּדוּ אֶת דּוֹרָם לָדַעַת אֶת ה' כְּאַבְרָהָם מֹשֶׁה וּשְׁמוּאֵל וְזוּלָתָם, כְּאָמְרָם זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "עֵילָם וְהֵם דָּנִיֵּאל וַחֲבֵרָיו זָכְתָה לִלְמוֹד וְלֹא זָכְתָה לְלַמֵּד" (פסחים פז:). וְכֵן נֹחַ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוֹכִיחַ עַל הַמַּעֲשִׂים הַמְקֻלְקָלִים עִנְיַן הַמְּדִינוֹת, לֹא הוֹרָה אוֹתָם לָדַעַת הָאֵל יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלָלֶכֶת בִּדְרָכָיו, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא הָיָה צַדִּיק תָּמִים בָּעִיּוּן וּבַמַּעֲשֶׂה. כִּי אָמְנָם צַדִּיק הַמַּשְׁלִים עַצְמוֹ בִּלְבַד הוּא רָאוּי שֶׁיִּמָּלֵט עַצְמוֹ בִּלְבַד, אֲבָל הַמַּשְׁלִים גַּם אֶת זוּלָתוֹ הוּא רָאוּי שֶׁיִּמָּלֵט גַּם אֶת זוּלָתוֹ, כִּי בָּזֶה יֵשׁ תִּקְוָה שֶׁיַּחֲזִירֵם בִּתְשׁוּבָה, כְּאָמְרָם זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (ברכות יט.): "אִם רָאִיתָ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁסָּרַח בַּיּוֹם אַל תְּהַרְהֵר אַחֲרָיו בַּלַּיְלָה, שֶׁוַּדַּאי עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה". חסלת פרשת בראשית.
